Spin-Peierls instability of the U(1) Dirac spin liquid

Urban F. P. Seifert Thanks: These two authors contributed equally to this work. Affiliation: Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics, University of California, Santa Barbara, CA 93106    Josef Willsher Thanks: These two authors contributed equally to this work. Affiliation: Technical University of Munich, TUM School of Natural Sciences, Physics Department, 85748 Garching, Germany Affiliation: Munich Center for Quantum Science and Technology (MCQST), Schellingstr. 4, 80799 München, Germany    Markus Drescher Affiliation: Technical University of Munich, TUM School of Natural Sciences, Physics Department, 85748 Garching, Germany Affiliation: Munich Center for Quantum Science and Technology (MCQST), Schellingstr. 4, 80799 München, Germany    Frank Pollmann Affiliation: Technical University of Munich, TUM School of Natural Sciences, Physics Department, 85748 Garching, Germany Affiliation: Munich Center for Quantum Science and Technology (MCQST), Schellingstr. 4, 80799 München, Germany    Johannes Knolle Affiliation: Technical University of Munich, TUM School of Natural Sciences, Physics Department, 85748 Garching, Germany Affiliation: Munich Center for Quantum Science and Technology (MCQST), Schellingstr. 4, 80799 München, Germany Affiliation: Blackett Laboratory, Imperial College London, London SW7 2AZ, United Kingdom
Abstract

A complicating factor in the realization and observation of quantum spin liquids in materials is the ubiquitous presence of other degrees of freedom, in particular lattice distortion modes (phonons). These provide additional routes for relieving magnetic frustration, thereby possibly destabilizing spin-liquid ground states. In this work, we focus on triangular-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnets, where recent numerical evidence suggests the presence of an extended U(1) Dirac spin liquid phase which is described by compact quantum electrodynamics in 2+1 dimensions (QED3), featuring gapless spinons and monopoles as gauge excitations, and believed to flow to a strongly-coupled fixed point with conformal symmetry. Using complementary perturbation theory and scaling arguments, we show that a symmetry-allowed coupling between (classical) finite-wavevector lattice distortions and monopole operators of the U(1) Dirac spin liquid generally induces a spin-Peierls instability towards a (confining) 12-site valence-bond solid state. We support our theoretical analysis with state-of-the-art density matrix renormalization group simulations. Away from the limit of static distortions, we demonstrate that the phonon energy gap establishes a parameter regime where the spin liquid is expected to be stable, and show that the monopole-lattice coupling leads to softening of the phonon in analogy to the Kohn anomaly. We discuss the applicability of our results to similar systems, in particular the Dirac spin liquid on the Kagome lattice.

I Introduction

The presence of many competing classical ground states in frustrated magnets implies that strong quantum fluctuations may stabilize quantum spin liquids (QSL) as highly exotic states of quantum matter. These states fall outside Landau’s paradigm of symmetry-breaking orders, and are instead characterized by a rich entanglement structure and described in terms of emergent deconfined gauge theories [1, 2, 3].

Recent years have witnessed remarkable progress in the theoretical description and classification of QSLs, as well as the experimental identification and characterization of candidate materials. However, while model spin systems have been studied using a variety of theoretical and numerical methods, definitive experimental evidence for the realization of a QSL phase in a material is still outstanding. Materials inevitably include additional spin-spin interactions, impurities and other sources of quenched disorder [4, 5, 6, 7], as well as the coupling of spins to additional degrees of freedom, for example lattice distortions. Given the competing nature of interactions in frustrated magnets [8], these perturbations can have a marked impact [9, 10, 11] on characteristic observable properties of QSLs realized in actual materials, or even mask such a phase completely, resulting in possibly complex phase diagrams of multiple competing orders [12, 13].

A paradigmatic example for the interplay of strong spin fluctuations and lattice degrees of freedom is given by the spin-Peierls instability of one-dimensional spin-1/2 chains: While the canonical antiferromagnetic Heisenberg chain possesses a gapless disordered ground state with power-law decaying correlations, an infinitesimally weak coupling to static lattice deformations leads to a finite dimerization and the concomitant opening of a spin gap [14, 15], since the energy gain of dimerization of the spin liquid outcompetes the harmonic elastic energy cost. This presupposes that the coupling of lattice distortion to the dimerization operator (instanton) of the effective Luttinger-liquid field theory for the S=1/2S=1/2 Heisenberg chain is symmetry-allowed and relevant. Accounting for intrinsic quantum dynamics of the lattice degrees of freedom (i.e. phonons with finite frequency), a finite interaction strength is required to induce the ordering transition [16, 17].

Turning to two-dimensional frustrated magnets, experiments show that magnetic phase transitions and the nature of magnetic ordering are often correlated with structural distortions which can act to (partially) relieve magnetic frustration. A crucial, long-standing question of immense experimental relevance concerns the stability of spin-liquid states against spin-lattice couplings. While numerical studies have found evidence for the presence of spin-Peierls-type instabilities in gapless spin-disordered phases [18, 19], there are only few analytical results for gapless spin-liquids, which have been mostly focused on intrinsic nesting instabilities of spinon Fermi surfaces [20, 21]. It is well understood that frustrated spin-systems may form valence bond solid (VBS) states via spontaneous symmetry breaking [22, 23]. However, a destabilization of a stable spin liquid ground state by dynamically generating lattice distortions, the true analog to the one-dimensional instability, has hereto not been investigated.

In the manuscript at hand, we consider the U(1) Dirac spin liquid (DSL) and make use of recent numerical and field-theoretic advances to investigate its stability against spin-lattice couplings. The DSL is a paradigmatic example of a QSL characterized by strongly interacting gapless spinons and U(1) gauge fluctuations which are described (at low energies) by compact quantum electrodynamics in 2+1 dimensions (QED3). Initially suggested as a candidate ground state for square-lattice cuprates [24], the DSL later gained support as describing the spin-disordered phase of frustrated Heisenberg antiferromagnets on kagome [25, 26, 27, 28, 29] and triangular lattices [30, 31, 32, 33].

At low energies, QED3 is believed to flow to a strongly coupled fixed point with conformal symmetry, allowing for the low-energy description of the U(1) DSL and its excitations in terms of a conformal field theory (CFT) [34, 35, 36, 37]. Crucially, for the DSL to be an intrinsically stable phase of matter, all relevant operators in this conformal field theory must transform non-trivially under the microscopic symmetries of the system, such that they cannot be generated during the symmetry-preserving flow from the UV to the IR.

The most relevant operators in the QED3 field theory are monopoles which can be understood as topological instanton events which tunnel an integer-2​π2\pi magnetic flux of the emergent U⁡(1)\mathrm{U(1)} gauge field. Proliferation of such monopoles corresponds to a confinement transition. As shown by Song et al. in Refs. [38, 39] and found in numerical simulations [33, 40], monopole operators transform under microscopic symmetries and can be identified with order parameters for Néel-ordered antiferromagnetic and VBS phases, which can hence be accessed via a proliferation of these monopole operators — the U(1) DSL state has therefore also been dubbed the “mother of competing orders” [41]. Importantly, the proliferation of monopoles on the triangular and kagome lattices is forbidden as long as the microscopic lattice symmetries are preserved, and on these lattices the DSL is expected to be stable.

The Luttinger liquid phase of 1+1 dimensional Heisenberg spin-half chains can also be said to be the mother of competing VBS and AFM orders [42]. Similarly it has an equivalent description in terms of Dirac fermions coupled to a dynamical U(1) gauge field [43, 44, 45] and therefore may be understood as a 1+1 dimensional analog to the DSL [38]. This analogy between theories will be our basis for extending the well-established spin-Peierls instability of spin chains to 2+1 dimensional QSLs.

In this work, we show that on the triangular lattice, there exists a symmetry-allowed coupling between monopoles and lattice deformations at certain (finite) wavevectors. Though the monopoles per se are relevant operators in the QED3 CFT and the coupling is symmetry-allowed, this does not necessarily imply an instability of the DSL, since there is an intrinsic (elastic) energy cost associated with a lattice distortion. For an instability coupling to occur (at nonzero coupling), the system must dynamically generate such a distortion by optimizing the competition between the elastic potential and the possible distortion-induced energy gain of the spin liquid.

Here, we exploit the conformal nature of the QED3 fixed point theory [37] and use both weak-coupling conformal perturbation theory as well as scaling approaches to analyze the coupled lattice-DSL system, and show that at zero temperature, any infinitesimally weak coupling gg induces a finite distortion of the underlying lattice and simultaneously precipitates monopole proliferation, leading the VBS order.

To make connection with experiment, we establish the phenomenology of the spin-Peierels instability of DSL and explicitly determine the symmetry of the lattice distortion and corresponding 12-site VBS-ordered state, as depicted in Figure 1. Our field-theoretic approach further allows us to determine critical temperatures for the ordering transition, which exhibit a non-trivial power-law dependence on the spin-lattice coupling TSP∼g1/(3−2​ΔΦ)T_{\mathrm{SP}}\sim g^{1/(3-2\Delta_{\Phi})} (with ΔΦ\Delta_{\Phi} denoting the scaling dimension of the monopole operator).

Guided by these theoretical predictions, we make use of state-of-the-art density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) [46, 47, 48] methods to numerically simulate the antiferromagnetic extended Heisenberg model on a distorted triangular lattice [30, 32, 49, 33]. We stabilize the DSL state on the undistorted geometry, and compare the energy gain of several lattice distortion patterns; we find that the largest energy gain is observed for the 12-site lattice distortion corresponding to the spin-Peierls transition from monopole condensation. We use finite-size scaling to argue that this is consistent with a zero-coupling instability in the thermodynamic limit as predicted by the field theory analysis.

Beyond the adiabatic approximation, where lattice deformations are considered static, finite phonon frequencies ω0\omega_{0} induce retarded monopole-monopole interactions. An analysis of the resulting effective action shows that there exists a finite parameter regime g2<c​ω03−2​ΔΦg^{2}<c\omega_{0}^{3-2\Delta_{\Phi}} where the DSL is expected to be stable (for some constant cc). Our work, therefore, places constraints on the experimental observability of U(1) Dirac spin liquids in systems with non-negligible spin-lattice couplings. As an additional experimental signature of the DSL in the stable regime we point out that the DSL-lattice coupling leads to a Kohn-type anomaly of the phonon spectrum.

The manuscript has the following structure. In Section II, we briefly review the Peierls instability in both free and interacting one-dimensional systems and discuss previous approaches to two-dimensional Peierls phases. Sec. III introduces the U⁡(1)\mathrm{U(1)} Dirac spin liquid ground state of the frustrated triangular-lattice Heisenberg model and its conformal field theory description. In Sec. IV we derive symmetry-allowed couplings between monopole operators in the effective theory of the DSL and lattice distortions. We investigate the spin-Peierls instability in Sec. V using complementary weak-coupling perturbation theoretic and scaling arguments. In Sec. VI we supplement our analytical insights with numerical DMRG results. Finally, in Sec VII we discuss the case of quantum (finite-frequency) phonons. We argue for a finite parameter window of stability and show that a temperature-dependent softening of the phonon dispersion provides a potentially accessible signature of the DSL. Sec. VIII concludes the paper and discusses the relevance of our results for recent triangular- and kagome-lattice QSL candidate materials.

II Recap of the spin-Peierls instability

II.1 Free spins & fermions

Peierls’ theorem can be succinctly summarized as stating that a chain of equally spaced ions with odd numbers of free fermions per site is unstable for any infinitesimal coupling to the lattice [50]. Considering a two-site lattice distortion ui=(−1)i​δ​uu_{i}=(-1)^{i}\delta u, the potential energy cost in the Harmonic approximation of the ions will be Helast=(K/2)​∑i(ui−ui+1)2H_{\mathrm{elast}}=(K/2)\sum_{i}(u_{i}-u_{i+1})^{2}, with lattice stiffness KK. This distortion has lattice wavevector k=π/2k=\pi/2 and is commensurate with the Fermi wavevector for a half-filled band of fermions. This lattice deformation correspondingly changes the fermion tight-binding hopping amplitudes at first order to ti=t+(−1)i​δ​tt_{i}=t+(-1)^{i}\delta t for δ​t/t=g⁡(δ​u/𝖺)\delta t/t=g(\delta u/\mathsf{a}), where 𝖺\mathsf{a} is the lattice spacing, and gg is a dimensionless constant which quantifies the change in overlap. The spectrum opens a band gap δ​t\delta t and the electronic energy of the lower occupied band is reduced; the total energy change is

E​(δ​u)free=EGS+(δ​u)2​[K−t​g22​𝖺2​log⁡(g2​(δ​u)2𝖺2)].E(\delta u)_{\mathrm{free}}=E_{\mathrm{GS}}+(\delta u)^{2}\left[K-\frac{t\,g^{2}}{2\mathsf{a}^{2}}\log(\frac{g^2 \, (\delta u)^2 }{\mathsf{a}^2})\right]. (1)

Due to the appearance of the logarithm in this approximation, the energy gain out-competes the cost of static lattice distortion and a finite equilibrium dimerization is developed δueq∼𝖺exp[−K𝖺2/(g2t)]\delta u_{\mathrm{eq}}\sim\mathsf{a}\exp[-{K\mathsf{a}^{2}}/{(g^{2}t)}], giving alternating strong and weak hopping amplitudes as seen in polyacetylene [51, 52]. The XY chain can be exactly mapped via the Jordan–Wigner transformation to free spinless one-dimensional fermions. The model’s gapless, spin-disordered ground state is destroyed by the spin-Peierls dimerization of the lattice at infinitesimal coupling [14, 15, 53]. The resulting valence-bond order of the spins consists of singlet states on each strong bond.

One can attempt to generalize the one-dimensional result by coupling gapless Dirac fermions in half-filled graphene to commensurate lattice distortions at the 𝑲{\bm{K}}-points. Indeed, the proposed Kekulé distortion of the underlying honeycomb lattice modulates the hopping amplitudes in exactly this way and opens up a gap in the Dirac spectrum [54, 55]. However, the electronic energy gain from the resulting gapped spectrum in 2D is not logarithmically divergent as in 1D, but finite because of the vanishing fermionic density of states at the Dirac points. It leads to a finite fermion-lattice coupling gc=[2​𝖺2​K/3​t]1/2>0g_{c}=[2\mathsf{a}^{2}K/3t]^{1/2}>0, below which there is no dimerisation in the ground state δ​ueq=0\delta u_{\mathrm{eq}}=0. Due to the absence of a weak-coupling Peierls instability, pure graphene does not show this Kekulé distortion (unless in the form of quasi-one-dimensional carbon nanotube [56]), but only engineered materials with sufficient interactions can induce it, for example using an atom-trap platform [54], surface disorder [57], or lithium ion intercalation [58, 59]. In the context of QSLs, recent work has shown that the emergent, free, gapless Majorana fermions of the Z2 Kitaev honeycomb-lattice QSL can be gapped by the same Kekulé distortion above a critical coupling to the lattice gc>0g_{c}>0 [60, 61].

II.2 Interacting spins in one dimension

We now move on to spin-Peierls instabilities of interacting systems, focusing on the 1D antiferromagnetic (J>0J>0) Heisenberg chain with the Hamiltonian

HHeis=J​∑iS→i⋅S→i+1,H_{\mathrm{Heis}}=J\sum_{i}\vec{S}_{i}\cdot\vec{S}_{i+1}, (2)

with SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU(2)} spin operators SαS^{\alpha}, α=x,y,z\alpha=x,y,z. It can be rewritten in terms of interacting spinless fermions via a Jordan–Wigner transformation. Within the bosonization framework [53, 17] it can be shown that the lowest-energy excitations correspond to fluctuations in the fermion density ∂xϕ⁡(x)\partial_{x}\phi(x) and phase. The resulting field theoretic Hamiltonian H⁡[ϕ⁡(x)]H[\phi(x)], where ϕ⁡(x)∈[0,2​π]\phi(x)\in[0,2\pi], takes the form of the Luttinger liquid:

H⁡[ϕ⁡(x)]=1π​∫d2x⁡[14​(∂tϕ)2+(∂xϕ)2]+V4​∫d2x​cos⁡(4​ϕ).H[\phi(x)]=\frac{1}{\pi}\int\differential[2]{x}\left[\frac{1}{4}(\partial_{t}\phi)^{2}+(\partial_{x}\phi)^{2}\right]+V_{4}\int\differential[2]{x}\cos(4\phi). (3)

The parameter V4V_{4} at the UV scale is fixed by the lattice parameter JJ. The kinetic term describes a Luttinger liquid, a free boson with fixed normalization 1/21/2 (see Appendix A for the general bosonization description of spin chains in terms of Luttinger liquids). The V4V_{4} coupling to the cosine represents an instanton term, which is marginally irrelevant, meaning the Heisenberg model has a gapless ground state.

The standard coupling of the spins to the lattice [62] is then given by

Hg=g​∑i(ui−ui+1)​S→i⋅S→i+1,H_{g}=g\sum_{i}(u_{i}-u_{i+1})\vec{S}_{i}\cdot\vec{S}_{i+1}, (4)

and is quantified by the coupling gg. The total Hamiltonian is given as the sum H=HHeis+Helast+HgH=H_{\mathrm{Heis}}+H_{\mathrm{elast}}+H_{g}. Bosonizing this interaction leads to a new instanton term in the effective theory

H⁡[u]=V2​∫d2x​sin⁡(2​ϕ),with​V2=g​δ​u,H[u]=V_{2}\int\differential[2]{x}\sin(2\phi),\quad\text{with}\,\,V_{2}=g\,\delta u, (5)

where the coupling V2V_{2} in the Heisenberg model has dimension Δ2=[V2]=1/2\Delta_{2}=[V_{2}]=1/2 which is more relevant than Δ4\Delta_{4}. Note that translating by one lattice constant i→i+1i\to i+1, we have sin⁡(2​ϕ)→−sin⁡(2​ϕ)\sin(2\phi)\to-\sin(2\phi) and δ​u→−δ​u\delta u\to-\delta u and the action still obeys translational symmetry by construction.

The mass scale generated by the coupling V2=g​δ​uV_{2}=g\,\delta u is given by (g​δ​u)χ/2(g\,\delta u)^{\chi/2} and the gapped ground state energy is lowered by (g​δ​u)χ(g\,\delta u)^{\chi} where χ=4/3\chi=4/3 for the AFM Heisenberg model. The ground state energy now depends on the distortion as

E​(δ​u)Heis=EGS+K​(δ​u)2−c​(g​δ​u)4/3E(\delta u)_{\mathrm{Heis}}=E_{\mathrm{GS}}+K(\delta u)^{2}-c(g\,\delta u)^{4/3} (6)

where cc is a constant. Due to the non-analytic behavior of the spin energy as a function of distortion, there is a solution that minimizes the free energy with a finite distortion δ​ueq∼(c​gχ/K)1/(2−χ).\delta u_{\mathrm{eq}}\sim(c\,g^{\chi}/K)^{1/(2-\chi)}. For χ<2\chi<2, this state has lower energy than δ​u=0\delta u=0. Hence, at zero temperature T=0T=0 and in the thermodynamic limit, a lattice distortion and concomitant spin dimerization is induced, as has additionally been confirmed by numerical DMRG simulations [63, 64].

At finite temperatures, the spin-Peierls instability competes with thermal fluctuations. Above a spin-Peierls temperature Tc=0.253​J​[g2/(𝖺2​K)]T_{c}=0.253\,J[g^{2}/(\mathsf{a}^{2}K)], no instability occurs [62]. It has widely been measured in experiments in materials that realize such quasi-one dimensional spin chain models [65, 66].

Furthermore, if one considers lattice distortions as quantum mechanical optical phonons, the spin-Peierls instability moves to finite coupling [17]. Optical phonons u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) with energy ω0\omega_{0} couple to the bosonized spins in the same way via ∫d2x​g​u​(x)​sin⁡(2​ϕ)\int\differential[2]{x}g\,u(x)\sin(2\phi). They generate the interaction −g2∫d2xcos⁡(4​ϕ)-g^{2}\int\differential[2]{x}\cos(4\phi) and kinetic terms when the high-energy modes are integrated out, shifting the value of V4V_{4} and the Luttinger parameter. At sufficient coupling, the induced effective interaction V4′V_{4}^{\prime} becomes relevant; a mass gap is induced and the spin-liquid destabilized above a critical coupling gc∼ω03/2g_{c}\sim\omega_{0}^{3/2} [67].

III U(1) Dirac spin liquids

In the following, for concreteness, we focus on the DSL on a triangular lattice, which may be realized in the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} Heisenberg model

H=J1​∑⟨i,j⟩S→i⋅S→j+J2​∑⟨⟨i,j⟩⟩S→i⋅S→j,H=J_{1}\sum_{\left<i,j\right>}\vec{S}_{i}\cdot\vec{S}_{j}+J_{2}\sum_{\left<\left<i,j\right>\right>}\vec{S}_{i}\cdot\vec{S}_{j}, (7)

where J1J_{1} and J2J_{2} are nearest- and next-nearest-neighbour antiferromagnetic exchange couplings. Numerical studies indicate that a spin liquid phase is realized around the classically-disordered point of J2/J1=1/8J_{2}/J_{1}=1/8 [30], with recent numerical evidence pointing towards a U⁡(1)\mathrm{U(1)} Dirac spin liquid [32, 49, 33]. For reference, we define the triangular lattice vectors

𝒂1=𝖺​(1,0)⊤and𝒂2=𝖺​(1/2,3/2)⊤,{\bm{a}}_{1}=\mathsf{a}(1,0)^{\top}\quad\text{and}\quad{\bm{a}}_{2}=\mathsf{a}(1/2,\sqrt{3}/2)^{\top}, (8)

where 𝖺\mathsf{a} denotes the lattice constant, and the nearest-neighbor vectors are labeled 𝜹1=𝒂2−𝒂1{\bm{\delta}}_{1}={\bm{a}}_{2}-{\bm{a}}_{1}, 𝜹2=𝒂1{\bm{\delta}}_{2}={\bm{a}}_{1} and 𝜹3=−𝒂2{\bm{\delta}}_{3}=-{\bm{a}}_{2} as depicted in Fig. 2. The corresponding reciprocal lattice vectors are

𝒈1=(2π,−2π/3)⊤/𝖺and𝒈2=(0,4π/3)⊤/𝖺.{\bm{g}}_{1}=(2\pi,-2\pi/\sqrt{3})^{\top}/\mathsf{a}\quad\text{and}\quad{\bm{g}}_{2}=(0,4\pi/\sqrt{3})^{\top}/\mathsf{a}. (9)

The high-symmetry points of the hexagonal Brillouin zone are indicated in Fig. 2, and the 𝑲a{\bm{K}}_{a} points are explicitly

𝑲1,3=[4π/3𝖺](1/2,∓3/2)and𝑲2=[4π/3𝖺](−1,0).{\bm{K}}_{1,3}=[4\pi/3\mathsf{a}](1/2,\mp\sqrt{3}/2)\quad\text{and}\quad{\bm{K}}_{2}=[4\pi/3\mathsf{a}](-1,0). (10)

III.1 QED3 effective theory

In a parton mean-field description, one can rewrite spin-operators in terms of fermionic partons fi,τf_{i,\tau} as S→i=fi,α†​σ→α​β​fi,β\vec{S}_{i}=f_{i,\alpha}^{\dagger}\vec{\sigma}_{\alpha\beta}f_{i,\beta} and perform a subsequent decoupling of spin-spin interactions in the microscopic Hamiltonian (7). The fermionic parton construction introduces unphysical degrees of freedom which can be projected out by enforcing the unit-occupancy constraint fi,↑†​fi,↑+fi,↓†​fi,↓​=!​1f_{i,\uparrow}^{\dagger}f_{i,\uparrow}+f_{i,\downarrow}^{\dagger}f_{i,\downarrow}\overset{!}{=}1 on each site. This leads to the emergence of a dynamical U(1) gauge field ai​ja_{ij}. The DSL state is then defined by the mean-field Hamiltonian

ℋDSL=∑α=↑,↓∑i,jχi​j​fi,α†​fj,α\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{DSL}}=\sum_{\alpha=\uparrow,\downarrow}\sum_{i,j}\chi_{ij}f_{i,\alpha}^{\dagger}f_{j,\alpha} (11)

where the ansatz χi​j\chi_{ij} consists of the fermions (spinons) hopping in a staggered π\pi-flux background of the dynamical gauge field [31]. Under U⁡(1)\mathrm{U(1)} gauge transformations, the fermions transform as fj→ei​θj​fjf_{j}\to\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta_{j}}f_{j}, the gauge field transforms as ai​j→ai​j−θi+θja_{ij}\to a_{ij}-\theta_{i}+\theta_{j}, and the mean-field Hamiltonian as χi​j↦χi​j​ei​ai​j\chi_{ij}\mapsto\chi_{ij}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}a_{ij}}. Note that this implies that ai​j∈[0,2​π]a_{ij}\in[0,2\pi]; the gauge group is compact.

The spectrum of the resulting fermion Hamiltonian features two Dirac cones per spin at two distinct momenta in the hexagonal Brillouin zone. At low energies (long wavelengths), this gives rise to an additional SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU(2)} valley degree of freedom; one can pass over to a continuum description, with the Lagrangian (in Euclidean signature)

ℒQED3=−∑i=14ψ¯iγμ(∂μ−iaμ)ψi+14​g2fμ​νfμ​ν,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}=-\sum_{i=1}^{4}\overline{\psi}_{i}\gamma^{\mu}(\partial_{\mu}-\mathrm{i}a_{\mu})\psi_{i}+\frac{1}{4g^{2}}f_{\mu\nu}f^{\mu\nu}, (12)

describing Dirac fermions with N=4N=4 flavors (2 spin ×\times 2 valley) minimally coupled to a U(1) gauge field aμa_{\mu} with field-strength tensor fμ​νf_{\mu\nu}, thus corresponding to Quantum Electrodynamics in 2+1-dimensions.

Note that in the low-energy theory ℒQED3\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}, the spin- and valley symmetries SU​(2)spin×SU​(2)valley\mathrm{SU(2)}_{\mathrm{spin}}\times\mathrm{SU(2)}_{\mathrm{valley}} become enhanced to a global SU⁡(4)\mathrm{SU(4)} symmetry acting on the flavor degrees of freedom of the Dirac fermions. Further, the theory possesses Lorenz symmetry as well as discrete charge conjugation 𝒞\mathcal{C}, time reversal 𝒯\mathcal{T} and parity 𝒫\mathcal{P} symmetries.

In 2+1 dimensions, the coupling in Eq. (12) has mass dimension [g2]=1[g^{2}]=1, implying that the theory is strongly coupled in the infrared (IR), long-wavelength, limit. For a sufficiently large number of flavors NN, QED3\text{QED}_{3} is believed to flow to a strongly-coupled IR-fixed point with conformal symmetry [34, 68]. In the remainder of this work we assume that this fixed point is realized also for N=4N=4 [69, 70] and that spontaneous chiral symmetry breaking does not occur [71, 72, 73] for Eq. (7).

III.2 Monopole operators

As written above, the low-energy theory ℒQED3\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}} appears to have an additional global symmetry U​(1)topo\mathrm{U(1)}_{\mathrm{topo}} with the conserved current jtopoμ=12​π​ϵμ​ν​ρ​∂νaρj_{\mathrm{topo}}^{\mu}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho}\partial_{\nu}a_{\rho}, corresponding to the conservation of magnetic flux (hence sometimes referred to as ‘magnetic symmetry’). However, given that ℒQED3\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}} emerges as the low-energy description of a compact U⁡(1)\mathrm{U(1)} lattice gauge theory, instanton events may add/remove integer-qq multiples of 2​π2\pi magnetic flux. The corresponding operators are referred to as monopole operators ℳ2​π​q†\mathcal{M}^{\dagger}_{2\pi q} [74], and are charged under the U​(1)topo\mathrm{U(1)}_{\mathrm{topo}}. These monopole operators do not possess an explicit representation as some polynomial in the gauge-field aμa_{\mu} and spinons ψ\psi [74, 38], but rather correspond to topologically non-trivial gauge field configurations [36]. From the lattice perspective, this 2​π2\pi flux insertion can be, for example on the torus, understood as modifying the π\pi-flux mean-field state by spreading a uniform 2​π/L22\pi/L^{2} flux in each unit cell [75, 29].

It is well known that pure compact U⁡(1)\mathrm{U(1)} gauge theory is unstable towards confinement due to the proliferation of monopoles [76]. In the context of the U(1) gauge theory coupled to N=4N=4 gapless fermions, the question of stability is more involved. The monopoles can be schematically written as Φa†∼f†​f†​ℳ2​π†\Phi^{\dagger}_{a}\sim f^{\dagger}f^{\dagger}\mathcal{M}_{2\pi}^{\dagger} with a=1​…​6a=1\dots 6 corresponding to six ways of half-filling four Dirac zero modes ff, as mandated by gauge invariance [38]. These monopoles transform under a six-dimensional representation of SU⁡(4)\mathrm{SU(4)}. Understanding the stability of the system requires understanding if monopole excitations Φa\Phi_{a} are (1) relevant perturbations to the IR fixed point and (2) allowed by the microscopic symmetries of the system:

  1. (1)

    Both analytical [36] as well as numerical studies [35] point towards monopoles being strongly relevant for QED3\text{QED}_{3} with N=4N=4 flavors, with a recent bootstrap [37] calculation suggesting a monopole scaling dimension ΔΦ≃1.02\Delta_{\Phi}\simeq 1.02 (we adopt the convention that [Φ]∼L−ΔΦ[\Phi]\sim L^{-\Delta_{\Phi}} with some length scale LL, e.g. the system size, so that ΔΦ<2+1\Delta_{\Phi}<2+1 implies relevance in 2+1 dim.).

  2. (2)

    On the triangular lattice all six monopole operators have non-trivial quantum numbers under the UV symmetries of the system [38, 39]. Hence, as long as these lattice symmetries are preserved, single-monopoles are not allowed and no ordering instability via monopole proliferation will occur. In contrast, on the square and honeycomb lattice, there exists a trivial (symmetry-allowed) monopole operator, such that the DSL state on these lattices is unstable.

We include a brief overview of the application of conformal field theory to the description of the DSL IR fixed point for completeness in Appendix B. The power of this approach comes from being able to describe the fixed point by a spectrum of primary operators 𝒪i\mathcal{O}_{i}, with the knowlege of their scaling dimensions Δi\Delta_{i} and symmetry transformation properties. By conformal invariance, two-point correlation functions (in Euclidean spacetime) of primaries can then be written exactly as

⟨𝒪i​(x)​𝒪j​(y)⟩=δi​j|x−y|2​Δi.\langle\mathcal{O}_{i}(x)\mathcal{O}_{j}(y)\rangle=\frac{\delta_{ij}}{|x-y|^{2\Delta_{i}}}. (13)

The conformal theory is fully described by this spectrum of operators alongside an understanding of how they combine — this is provided by the operator product expansion (OPE). Within our scheme we focus on the most-relevant charge-one monopoles Φ\Phi and the leading-order OPE can be summarized as Φ†×Φ∼𝟙+⋯\Phi^{\dagger}\times\Phi\sim\mathds{1}+\cdots.

While the above discussion was focused on monopole proliferation, there may exist other perturbations that constitute relevant deformations to the IR fixed point, such as fermion bilinears (see also Appendix B). However, as discussed in Refs. [38, 39], on the triangular lattice, these perturbations are also either irrelevant or symmetry-forbidden. The leading symmetry-allowed operator is a monopole which inserts 6​π6\pi topological flux and is expected to be irrelevant; as such the DSL on the triangular lattice is expected to be stable.

IV Monopole-lattice coupling

In this section, we derive the effective theory of a lattice distortions coupled to monopole operators in QED3\text{QED}_{3}. This is based on a symmetry analysis facilitated by the knowledge of the symmetry quantum numbers of monopole operators on the triangular lattice [38, 39, 77].

IV.1 Monopole symmetry quantum numbers

The monopoles Φa\Phi_{a} form a six-dimensional representation of the IR-symmetry group SU⁡(4)\mathrm{SU(4)}. The two (independent) microscopic symmetries SU​(2)valley\mathrm{SU(2)}_{\mathrm{valley}} and SU​(2)spin\mathrm{SU(2)}_{\mathrm{spin}} as subgroups of SU⁡(4)\mathrm{SU(4)} correspond to mutually commuting SO​(3)valley\mathrm{SO(3)}_{\mathrm{valley}} and SO​(3)spin\mathrm{SO(3)}_{\mathrm{spin}} subgroups of SO⁡(6)\mathrm{SO}(6), such that we can decompose Φa\Phi_{a} into ‘valley-triplet, spin-singlet’ (a=1,2,3a=1,2,3) and ‘valley-singlet, spin-triplet’ components (a=4,5,6a=4,5,6).

Importantly, microscopic (lattice) UV symmetries such as translations, discrete rotations, and reflections are embedded in the enlarged symmetry group of the IR theory (in other words, microscopic symmetries are not broken in the flow to the IR fixed point). The monopole operators Φa\Phi_{a} carry non-trivial quantum numbers under lattice symmetries, which have been determined in Refs. [38, 39]. In Tab. 1 we reproduce the transformation of monopoles on the triangular lattice under discrete lattice translations TjT_{j} by unit vectors 𝒂j{\bm{a}}_{j}, reflections RR in the vertical direction, discrete rotations C6C_{6}, and time reversal 𝒯\mathcal{T}. The three valley-triplet monopoles (a=1,2,3a=1,2,3) carry the same quantum numbers as order parameters of valence-bond solids on the triangular lattice with lattice momenta 𝒌a=−𝑲a/2{\bm{k}}_{a}=-{\bm{K}}_{a}/2, respectively. Hence, we can write (up to a global multiplicative constant not fixed by symmetry)

S→i⋅S→i+𝜹a≃sa​Re⁡[Φa​(𝒓i)​ei​𝒌a⋅𝒓i],\vec{S}_{i}\cdot\vec{S}_{i+{\bm{\delta}}_{a}}\simeq s_{a}\operatorname{Re}[\Phi_{a}({\bm{r}}_{i})\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}{\bm{k}}_{a}\cdot{\bm{r}}_{i}}], (14)

where we introduce the sign factors sa=(+1,+1,−1)s_{a}=(+1,+1,-1) which are needed to reproduce the relative negative sign for Φ3\Phi_{3} in Tab. 1. The three spin-triplet monopoles (a=4,5,6a=4,5,6) transform identically as order parameters for antiferromagnetic 120∘120^{\circ} Néel order which determine the spin density as

Siα≃Re⁡[i​Φ3+α​(𝒓i)​ei​𝑲α⋅𝒓i],S_{i}^{\alpha}\simeq\operatorname{Re}[\mathrm{i}\Phi_{3+\alpha}({\bm{r}}_{i})\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}{\bm{K}}_{\alpha}\cdot{\bm{r}}_{i}}], (15)

where α=x,y,z\alpha=x,y,z (1,2,3) denotes the three SU​(2)spin\mathrm{SU(2)}_{\mathrm{spin}} components. (Note that the LHS in Eqs. (14) and (15) only correspond to the “lowest-order” microscopic expressions that transform as the RHS under symmetry transformations, and one may find terms of multiple spin operators that exhibit the same symmetry operators.) These expressions gives way to the interpretation of the monopoles as disorder operators [74], with their proliferation ⟨Φa⟩≠0\langle\Phi^{a}\rangle\neq 0 yielding conventionally ordered phases. Crucially, the nature of the phase is determined by the proliferating components of Φa\Phi_{a} and the corresponding broken global symmetries.

IV.2 Lattice deformation

We first neglect any quantum dynamics of lattice distortions and focus on classical displacement fields. Considering actual materials, this approximation is justified if phonons have a large inertial mass m0→∞m_{0}\to\infty such that the phonon frequency vanishes ω0→0\omega_{0}\to 0. In the literature on the spin-Peierls transition in one-dimensional systems, this is commonly referred to as the static phonon limit or the ‘adiabatic approximation’ [78, 16, 67].

Our starting point is the observation that the valley-triplet (spin-singlet) monopoles Φa\Phi_{a} (a=1,2,3a=1,2,3), which act as order parameters for VBSs, have lattice momenta 𝒌a=−𝑲a/2{\bm{k}}_{a}=-{\bm{K}}_{a}/2. Using Tab. 1, we note that the following deformation to the DSL fixed point is symmetry-allowed,

ℋ∼(ei​𝒌1⋅𝑹Φ1+ei​𝒌2⋅𝑹Φ2−ei​𝒌3⋅𝑹Φ3+h.c.).\mathcal{H}\sim\left(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}{\bm{k}}_{1}\cdot{\bm{R}}}\Phi_{1}+\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}{\bm{k}}_{2}\cdot{\bm{R}}}\Phi_{2}-\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}{\bm{k}}_{3}\cdot{\bm{R}}}\Phi_{3}+\mathrm{h.c.}\right). (16)

We emphasize that care must be taken in separating length scales: 𝑹{\bm{R}} (𝒌a{\bm{k}}_{a}) are coordinates (wavevectors) on the order of microscopic length scales such as the lattice constant 𝖺\mathsf{a}, where the Φa\Phi_{a} transform as given in Tab. 1. The scaling nature of the Φa\Phi_{a} as primaries in a CFT, and the corresponding power-law form of correlation functions (13) only holds on much longer lengthscales (and, equivalently, sufficiently small momenta), where a low-energy continuum formulation becomes justified. While Eq. (16) is symmetry allowed, the oscillating prefactors average out on sufficiently long length scales, such that the perturbation is strongly irrelevant.

We now consider an in-plane deformation of the real-space lattice 𝑹→𝒙=𝑹+𝒖⁡(𝒙){\bm{R}}\to{\bm{x}}={\bm{R}}+{\bm{u}}({\bm{x}}), where 𝒖⁡(𝒙){\bm{u}}({\bm{x}}) is a displacement field, as shown in the left panel of Fig. 1. Note that we work in implicitly-defined (Eulerian) coordinates of the deformed system 𝒙{\bm{x}}.

Expanding Eq. (16) to the first non-trivial order in |𝒖⁡(𝒙)|/𝖺≪1|{\bm{u}}({\bm{x}})|/\mathsf{a}\ll 1 (assuming that lattice distortions are small compared to the lattice constant 𝖺\mathsf{a}), we obtain the monopole-lattice coupling Hamiltonian

ℋg[𝒖(𝒙)]=g∑a=1,2,3sa[(i𝒌a⋅𝒖(𝒙))ei​𝒌a⋅𝒙Φa+h.c.],\mathcal{H}_{g}[{\bm{u}}({\bm{x}})]=g\sum_{a=1,2,3}s_{a}\left[\left(\mathrm{i}{\bm{k}}_{a}\cdot{\bm{u}}({\bm{x}})\right)\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}{\bm{k}}_{a}\cdot{\bm{x}}}\Phi_{a}+\mathrm{h.c.}\right], (17)

where we use again the sign factors sa=(+1,+1,−1)s_{a}=(+1,+1,-1) for convenience of notation. We have dropped the 0-th order terms (with oscillating phases) in the expansion. Note that i​𝒌a⋅𝒖\mathrm{i}{\bm{k}}_{a}\cdot{\bm{u}} transforms as a scalar under point-group operations RR and C6C_{6} and is appropriately even under time reversal 𝒯\mathcal{T}; therefore the prefactor retains the full symmetry of the undistorted system Eq. (16). With Eq. (14), this interaction can be seen as a modulation of the nearest-neighbor J1J_{1} coupling through the difference of site-spacing in the following way:

Hg​[𝒖i]≃g~​∑i∑a=1,2,3𝒌a⋅[𝒖⁡(𝒓i)−𝒖⁡(𝒓i+𝜹a)]​S→𝒓i⋅S→𝒓i+𝜹a.H_{g}[{\bm{u}}_{i}]\simeq\tilde{g}\sum_{i}\sum_{a=1,2,3}{\bm{k}}_{a}\cdot[{\bm{u}}({\bm{r}}_{i})-{\bm{u}}({\bm{r}}_{i}+{\bm{\delta}}_{a})]\,\vec{S}_{{\bm{r}}_{i}}\cdot\vec{S}_{{\bm{r}}_{i}+{\bm{\delta}}_{a}}. (18)

We can expand the real-component distortion field 𝒖⁡(𝒙){\bm{u}}({\bm{x}}) in eigenstates of the lattice momentum 𝒖𝑸{\bm{u}}_{\bm{Q}}

𝒖⁡(𝒙)=∑𝑸ei​𝑸⋅𝒙​𝒖𝑸,{\bm{u}}({\bm{x}})=\sum_{\bm{Q}}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}{\bm{Q}}\cdot{\bm{x}}}{\bm{u}}_{\bm{Q}}, (19)

where reality of 𝒖⁡(𝒙){\bm{u}}({\bm{x}}) implies 𝒖𝑸=𝒖−𝑸∗{\bm{u}}_{\bm{Q}}={\bm{u}}_{-{\bm{Q}}}^{\ast}. In momentum space, the coupling to monopoles is of the form

ℋg[𝒖(𝒙)]=g∑a=1,2,3∑𝑸sa[(i𝒌a⋅𝒖𝑸)ei⁡(𝒌a+𝑸)⋅𝒙Φa+h.c.].\mathcal{H}_{g}[{\bm{u}}({\bm{x}})]=g\sum_{a=1,2,3}\sum_{\bm{Q}}s_{a}\left[\left(\mathrm{i}{\bm{k}}_{a}\cdot{\bm{u}}_{\bm{Q}}\right)\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}({\bm{k}}_{a}+{\bm{Q}})\cdot{\bm{x}}}\Phi_{a}+\mathrm{h.c.}\right]. (20)

Crucially, only terms with 𝑸=−𝒌a{\bm{Q}}=-{\bm{k}}_{a} do not contain any oscillating prefactors and will thus be the ones relevant at the lowest energies; these are

ℋg[𝒖(𝒙)]=g∑a=1,2,3sa[(i𝒌a⋅𝒖𝒌a∗)Φa+h.c.].\mathcal{H}_{g}[{\bm{u}}({\bm{x}})]=g\sum_{a=1,2,3}s_{a}\left[\left(\mathrm{i}{\bm{k}}_{a}\cdot{\bm{u}}^{*}_{{\bm{k}}_{a}}\right)\Phi_{a}+\mathrm{h.c.}\right]. (21)

Our key observation is that, in analogy to the one-dimensional spin-Peierls transition, these terms may precipitate an instability. Indeed we will go on to use energetic arguments to establish the same result in the two-dimensional DSL. The response of QED3\text{QED}_{3} to this perturbation will be dominated by lattice distortions with crystal momentum 𝒌a{\bm{k}}_{a}. We highlight the translational invariance of (21) by noting that under translation, 𝒖𝒌a∗→ei​𝒌a⋅𝒂​𝒖𝒌a∗{\bm{u}}^{*}_{{\bm{k}}_{a}}\to\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}{\bm{k}}_{a}\cdot{\bm{a}}}{\bm{u}}^{*}_{{\bm{k}}_{a}}, and the coupling is unchanged, just like for the Heisenberg chain (see Appendix A).

IV.3 Elastic energy

We model lattice distortions as having a potential energy that is quadratic in the relative displacement between nearest neighbor sites,

Hph=K2​∑⟨i​j⟩|𝒖⁡(𝒙i)−𝒖⁡(𝒙j)|2.H_{\mathrm{ph}}=\frac{K}{2}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\left|{\bm{u}}({\bm{x}}_{i})-{\bm{u}}({\bm{x}}_{j})\right|^{2}. (22)

Here, KK takes the role of an effective spring constant for the displacement between atoms on the triangular lattice. Taking the continuum limit, inserting (19), and decomposing into transverse and longitudinal polarizations 𝒖𝒒=∑s=t,lϵ𝒒,s​u𝒒,s{\bm{u}}_{{\bm{q}}}=\sum_{s=t,l}{\bm{\epsilon}}_{{\bm{q}},s}u_{{\bm{q}},s} yields the Hamiltonian density

ℋph​[𝒖]=∑𝒒𝒦𝒒​|𝒖𝒒|2=∑𝒒,s𝒦𝒒​|u𝒒,s|2𝒦𝒒=2​K3​𝖺2​(3−[cos⁡(𝖺​qx)+2​cos⁡(𝖺​qx2)​cos⁡(3​𝖺​qy2)]).\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{ph}}[{\bm{u}}]=\sum_{{\bm{q}}}\mathcal{K}_{{\bm{q}}}|{\bm{u}}_{{\bm{q}}}|^{2}=\sum_{{\bm{q}},s}\mathcal{K}_{{\bm{q}}}|u_{{\bm{q}},s}|^{2}\\ \quad\mathcal{K}_{{\bm{q}}}=\frac{2K}{3\mathsf{a}^{2}}\left(3-\left[\cos( \mathsf{a} q_x)+2\cos(\frac{\mathsf{a} q_x}{2})\cos(\frac{\sqrt{3} \mathsf{a} q_y}{2})\right]\right). (23)

The polarization vectors ϵ𝒒,s{\bm{\epsilon}}_{{\bm{q}},s} are orthonormal, where the longitudinal direction is defined as ϵ𝒒,l=𝒒/|𝒒|{\bm{\epsilon}}_{{\bm{q}},l}={\bm{q}}/|{\bm{q}}|. Importantly, the complex scalar modes u𝒒,su_{{\bm{q}},s} are independent and degenerate, meaning the Hamiltonian of the longitudinal modes can be seperated. The energy density cost of a distortion goes to zero at the center of the Brillouin zone and is of order K/𝖺2K/\mathsf{a}^{2} towards the zone edges.

V DSL spin-Peierls instability

V.1 Conformal perturbation theory

V.1.1 IR Regularization

Our main goal is to study whether the phonon-monopole coupling generates an instability. To this end, we compute the energy of QED3\text{QED}_{3} in the background of arbitrary displacement fields 𝒖⁡(x){\bm{u}}(x) and extremize the resulting energy functional. It is convenient to employ a path-integral formulation, where we obtain a functional for the effective energy density ℰ=E/V\mathcal{E}=E/V (per volume VV) via the zero-temperature limit of the free energy,

ℰQED3​[𝒖]=1V​limβ→∞FQED3​[𝒖].\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}[{\bm{u}}]=\frac{1}{V}\lim_{\beta\to\infty}F_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}[{\bm{u}}]. (24)

The free energy of QED3\text{QED}_{3} coupled to some background displacement field 𝒖⁡(x){\bm{u}}(x),

FQED3​[𝒖]=−1β​log⁡𝒵QED3Sβ1×Σ​[𝒖],F_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}[{\bm{u}}]=-\frac{1}{\beta}\log\mathcal{Z}_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}^{S^{1}_{\beta}\times\Sigma}[{\bm{u}}], (25)

is given in terms of the partition function

𝒵QED3Sβ1×Σ​[𝒖]=∫𝒟⁡[{𝒪CFT}]​e−SQED3−Sg​[𝒖]\mathcal{Z}_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}^{S^{1}_{\beta}\times\Sigma}[{\bm{u}}]=\int\mathcal{D}[\{\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{CFT}}\}]\,\mathrm{e}^{-S_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}-S_{g}[{\bm{u}}]} (26)

with the respective actions SA=∫0βd​τ​LAS_{A}=\int_{0}^{\beta}\mathrm{d}\tau L_{A} on the manifold Sβ1×ΣS^{1}_{\beta}\times\Sigma. Here, Sβ1S^{1}_{\beta} corresponds to a circle in the imaginary time direction with circumference inverse temperature β=1/T\beta=1/T, and Σ\Sigma is some spatial manifold (for example a 2-sphere with radius LL, SL2S^{2}_{L}). We mostly focus on the thermodynamic limit Σ=limL→∞SL2=ℝ2\Sigma=\lim_{L\to\infty}S^{2}_{L}=\mathbb{R}^{2} (note that the partition function 𝒵=𝒵SL3\mathcal{Z}=\mathcal{Z}^{S^{3}_{L}} may also be defined on a 3-sphere with radius LL, see, e.g., Ref. 79, making the conformal SO⁡(3)\mathrm{SO}(3) symmetry group manifest).

Away from the large-NN limit, QED3\text{QED}_{3} is not solvable, and thus 𝒵QED3\mathcal{Z}_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}} cannot be computed exactly. Instead, we use (26) mainly as a computational framework. The schematic notation of the measure of the path integral indicates that all operators at the QED3\text{QED}_{3} CFT are to be integrated over. We will not attempt a rigorous definition here, as there is no explicit form for SQED3S_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}} in terms of CFT operators available.

V.1.2 Weak coupling analysis

In the limit of weak coupling we can work perturbatively and exploit the fact that two-point functions at the CFT fixed point are known. We assume that the monopole-lattice action is a small perturbation, justified by assuming small coupling gg and by our previous assumption that |𝒌a⋅𝒖𝑸|≪1|{\bm{k}}_{a}\cdot{\bm{u}}_{{\bm{Q}}}|\ll 1. Expanding the Boltzmann weight to quadratic order and taking the logarithm, we have

log⁡𝒵QED3​[𝒖]=log⁡𝒵QED3−⟨Sg⟩QED3+12​(⟨Sg2⟩QED3−⟨Sg⟩QED32)+…,\log\mathcal{Z}_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}[{\bm{u}}]=\log\mathcal{Z}_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}-\langle S_{g}\rangle_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}\\ +\frac{1}{2}\left(\langle S_{g}^{2}\rangle_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}-\langle S_{g}\rangle_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}^{2}\right)+\dots, (27)

where the expectation values are to be taken with respect to the path integral (26) with 𝒖≡0{\bm{u}}\equiv 0. At finite temperatures β<∞\beta<\infty, one-point functions of conformal primaries are generically non-zero ⟨𝒪⟩∼β−Δ𝒪\langle\mathcal{O}\rangle\sim\beta^{-\Delta_{\mathcal{O}}} [80], but, importantly, vanish in the zero-temperature limit β→∞\beta\to\infty, as also mandated by conformal invariance on ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}. Because we will primarily focus on the zero-temperature limit, we henceforth take ⟨Sg⟩QED3=0\langle S_{g}\rangle_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}=0.

The first non-trivial contribution to ℰQED3​[𝒖]\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}[{\bm{u}}] thus occurs at quadratic order (we use the notation x=(τx,𝒙)x=(\tau_{x},{\bm{x}}) for vectors in 2+1-dim. Euclidean spacetime),

⟨Sg2⟩QED3\displaystyle\langle S_{g}^{2}\rangle_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}} =g2∑a,bsasb∑𝑸,𝑸′∫Sβ1×Σd3xd3y[(i𝒌a⋅𝒖𝑸)ei⁡(𝒌a+𝑸)⋅𝒙(−i𝒌b⋅𝒖𝑸′∗)e−i(𝒌b+𝑸′)⋅𝒚⟨Φa(x)Φb†(y)⟩QED3+h.c.]\displaystyle=g^{2}\sum_{a,b}s_{a}s_{b}\sum_{{\bm{Q}},{\bm{Q}}^{\prime}}\int_{S^{1}_{\beta}\times\Sigma}\mathrm{d}^{3}x\mathrm{d}^{3}y\left[(\mathrm{i}{\bm{k}}_{a}\cdot{\bm{u}}_{{\bm{Q}}})\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}({\bm{k}}_{a}+{\bm{Q}})\cdot{\bm{x}}}(-\mathrm{i}{\bm{k}}_{b}\cdot{\bm{u}}_{{\bm{Q}}^{\prime}}^{\ast})\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}({\bm{k}}_{b}+{\bm{Q}}^{\prime})\cdot{\bm{y}}}\langle\Phi_{a}(x)\Phi_{b}^{\dagger}(y)\rangle_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}+\mathrm{h.c.}\right]
=g2βV∑a∫0βdτx′∫Σd2𝒙′[|𝒌a⋅𝒖𝑸|2ei⁡(𝒌a+𝑸)⋅𝒙′⟨Φa†(x′)Φa(0)⟩QED3+h.c.],\displaystyle=g^{2}\beta V\sum_{a}\int_{0}^{\beta}\mathrm{d}\tau_{x^{\prime}}\int_{\Sigma}\mathrm{d}^{2}{\bm{x}}^{\prime}\left[|{\bm{k}}_{a}\cdot{\bm{u}}_{\bm{Q}}|^{2}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}({\bm{k}}_{a}+{\bm{Q}})\cdot{\bm{x}}^{\prime}}\langle\Phi_{a}^{\dagger}(x^{\prime})\Phi_{a}(0)\rangle_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}+\mathrm{h.c.}\right], (28)

where V=vol⁡(Σ)=2​π​L2V=\mathrm{vol}(\Sigma)=2\pi L^{2} is a trivial factor of volume, mandated by the extensiveness. The thermodynamic limit Σ=ℝ2\Sigma=\mathbb{R}^{2} is obtained by taking the linear dimension L→∞L\to\infty. We have used in the above that monopole-monopole two-point functions ⟨Φa​(x)​Φb​(x)⟩QED3=0\langle\Phi_{a}(x)\Phi_{b}(x)\rangle_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}=0 vanish, monopole-antimonopole correlation functions are diagonal in the monopole flavor index, changed coordinates x′=x+yx^{\prime}=x+y and assumed translation invariance ⟨Φ†​(x+y)​Φ​(y)⟩QED3=⟨Φ​(x)†​Φ​(0)⟩QED3\langle\Phi^{\dagger}(x+y)\Phi(y)\rangle_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}=\langle\Phi(x)^{\dagger}\Phi(0)\rangle_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}.

For 𝑸≠−𝒌a{\bm{Q}}\neq-{\bm{k}}_{a} there exist rapidly oscillating terms in Eq. (28) (with momentum 𝒌a+𝑸{\bm{k}}_{a}+{\bm{Q}}), which, assuming that the monopole two-point function varies sufficiently slowly, produce finite contributions to ⟨Sg2⟩QED3\langle S_{g}^{2}\rangle_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}} which average out at sufficiently long length scales (in the continuum limit).

The term with 𝑸=−𝒌a{\bm{Q}}=-{\bm{k}}_{a} in Eq. (28) hence is the dominant contribution at low energies, which is due to the (relevant) coupling between monopoles and displacements at lattice momentum 𝒌a{\bm{k}}_{a}, as was written before in Eq. (21). This justifies us taking this interaction as the starting point for all further analysis.

We caution the reader that, while it may be tempting to immediately use the explicit expression for the conformal two-point function in Eq. (28), this is only justified at lowest energies, when there is a separation between microscopic (lattice) scales and slowly varying continuum fields, which is warranted in Eq. (28) only for 𝑸=−𝒌a{\bm{Q}}=-{\bm{k}}_{a} (otherwise, there is a finite transfer of lattice momentum).

The explicit form of the conformal two-point monopole correlation function in flat space reads ⟨Φa†​(x)​Φb​(0)⟩QED3=δa,b​|x|−2​ΔΦ\langle\Phi_{a}^{\dagger}(x)\Phi_{b}(0)\rangle_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}=\delta_{a,b}|x|^{-2\Delta_{\Phi}} [see also Eq. (13)]. As noted in Ref. [80], the cylindrical geometry is conformally flat in the L→∞L\to\infty limit, and OPEs converge for τ2+|𝒙2|<β→∞\sqrt{\tau^{2}+|{\bm{x}}^{2}|}<\beta\to\infty, such that we may use above form of the 2-pt. function to do the remaining integral. This integral is divergent in the thermodynamic, zero temperature limit, β,L→∞\beta,L\to\infty. At any other wavevector 𝑸≠−𝒌a{\bm{Q}}\neq-{\bm{k}}_{a}, the exponential in (28) cuts off the divergent integral and no instability occurs.

We regulate this divergence by working at finite temperatures β<∞\beta<\infty, which allows us to take the thermodynamic limit L→∞L\to\infty,

⟨Sg2⟩QED3β​V\displaystyle\frac{\langle S^{2}_{g}\rangle_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}}{\beta V} =2​g2​∑a∫0βd​τx​∫Σd2​𝒙​|𝒌a⋅𝒖𝒌a|2|τx2+|𝒙|2|ΔΦ\displaystyle=2g^{2}\sum_{a}\int_{0}^{\beta}\mathrm{d}\tau_{x}\int_{\Sigma}\mathrm{d}^{2}{\bm{x}}\,\frac{|{\bm{k}}_{a}\cdot{\bm{u}}_{{\bm{k}}_{a}}|^{2}}{|\tau_{x}^{2}+|{\bm{x}}|^{2}|^{\Delta_{\Phi}}}
=cΔΦ​g2​β3−2​ΔΦ​∑a|𝒌a⋅𝒖𝒌a|2\displaystyle=c_{\Delta_{\Phi}}g^{2}\beta^{3-2\Delta_{\Phi}}\sum_{a}|{\bm{k}}_{a}\cdot{\bm{u}}_{{\bm{k}}_{a}}|^{2} (29)

where we have introduced the numerical constant cΔΦ=2​π/[(ΔΦ−1)​(3−2​ΔΦ)]>0c_{\Delta_{\Phi}}=2\pi/[(\Delta_{\Phi}-1)(3-2\Delta_{\Phi})]>0 for 1<ΔΦ<3/21<\Delta_{\Phi}<3/2. For current estimates of the monopole scaling dimension this is true, and indeed this leads to a large numerical value cΔΦ≫1c_{\Delta_{\Phi}}\gg 1 because of the proximity of the monopole scaling dimension to one (ΔΦ−1)≪1(\Delta_{\Phi}-1)\ll 1 [36, 35, 37].

V.1.3 Spin-Peierls instability

We can now obtain the effective energy as a sum of the intrinsic potential energy cost of deformations at wavevectors 𝒌a{\bm{k}}_{a} and the relative energy gain of the DSL by coupling to the displacement field,

ℋeff​[𝒖]=ℋph​[𝒖]+(ℰQED3​[𝒖]−ℰQED3​[0])=∑a=1,2,3(κ​|𝒖𝒌a|2−limβ→∞cΔΦ​g2​β3−2​ΔΦ​|𝒌a⋅𝒖𝒌a|2)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{eff}}[{\bm{u}}]=\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{ph}}[{\bm{u}}]+\left(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}[{\bm{u}}]-\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}[0]\right)\\ =\sum_{a=1,2,3}\left(\kappa|{\bm{u}}_{{\bm{k}}_{a}}|^{2}-\lim_{\beta\to\infty}c_{\Delta_{\Phi}}g^{2}\beta^{3-2\Delta_{\Phi}}|{\bm{k}}_{a}\cdot{\bm{u}}_{{\bm{k}}_{a}}|^{2}\right) (30)

where we introduce κ=𝒦𝒌a\kappa=\mathcal{K}_{{\bm{k}}_{a}}. We observe that the second term in the parenthesis is minimized by taking lattice displacements that are longitudinal along the momenta 𝒖𝒌a=ua​𝒌a/|𝒌a|.{\bm{u}}_{{\bm{k}}_{a}}=u_{a}\,{\bm{k}}_{a}/|{\bm{k}}_{a}|. The scalar amplitudes uau_{a} are the longitudinal components u𝒌a,lu_{{\bm{k}}_{a},l} at the three independent displacement vectors 𝒌a{\bm{k}}_{a}. Henceforth we use the vector notation for these longitudinal displacements u→=(u1,u2,u3)⊤\vec{u}=(u_{1},u_{2},u_{3})^{\top}, such that we can express the effective potential in the form

ℋeff​[u→]=(κ−cΔΦ​g2​|𝒌a|2​β3−2​ΔΦ)​|u→|2.\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{eff}}[\vec{u}]=\left(\kappa-c_{\Delta_{\Phi}}g^{2}|{\bm{k}}_{a}|^{2}\beta^{3-2\Delta_{\Phi}}\right)|\vec{u}|^{2}. (31)

In the zero-temperature limit T=β−1→0T=\beta^{-1}\to 0 the effective energy density is not bounded from below for any finite (small) coupling g>0g>0, and hence the energy density diverges ℋeff→−∞\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{eff}}\to-\infty for any ua≠0u_{a}\neq 0. It is thus energetically preferable for the system to acquire a lattice distortion. We thus conclude that the coupling of valley-triplet monopoles (acting as VBS order parameters) to longitudinal displacement modes with wavevectors 𝒌a{\bm{k}}_{a} induces a weak-coupling instability of the DSL at low temperatures, analogous to the 1D spin-Peierls mechanism discussed in Section II.2.

The critical temperature scale TSP=1/βcT_{\mathrm{SP}}=1/\beta_{c} for the ordering instability is obtained by analyzing where the quadratic potential ℋeff​[u→]\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{eff}}[\vec{u}] [Eq. (31)] changes sign, yielding κ=cΔΦ​g2​βc3−2​ΔΦ​|𝒌a|2\kappa=c_{\Delta_{\Phi}}g^{2}\beta_{c}^{3-2\Delta_{\Phi}}|{\bm{k}}_{a}|^{2}. Recall that both the stiffness κ\kappa and the lattice momentum 𝒌a{\bm{k}}_{a} scale as the inverse of the lattice constant; we hence evaluate the critical spin Peierls temperature to be

TSP∼[1(ΔΦ−1)​g2K]1/(3−2​ΔΦ).T_{\mathrm{SP}}\sim\left[\frac{1}{(\Delta_{\Phi}-1)}\frac{g^{2}}{K}\right]^{1/(3-2\Delta_{\Phi})}. (32)

The VBS ground state is therefore separated from a high-temperature DSL phase by a finite-temperature spin-Peierls transition, again in analogy to the 1D case.

V.2 Scaling ansatz

In the above calculation, the weak-coupling approximation and expansion of the partition function apply when g2​|𝒌a|2​β3−2​ΔΦ​|u→|≪1g^{2}|{\bm{k}}_{a}|^{2}\beta^{3-2\Delta_{\Phi}}|\vec{u}|\ll 1. For stronger coupling gg or larger β→∞\beta\to\infty (or equivalently L→∞L\to\infty in the symmetric regularization), the first order perturbative expansion is not sufficient. In the following section, we take a complementary approach to the phonon-induced ordering instability by making a scaling approximation for the energy gain due to deforming QED3 by the coupling of monopoles to the classical displacement field. This applies in the opposite limit of strong coupling g2​|𝒌a|2​β3−2​ΔΦ​|u→|≫1g^{2}|{\bm{k}}_{a}|^{2}\beta^{3-2\Delta_{\Phi}}|\vec{u}|\gg 1.

We write the deformation to the QED3\text{QED}_{3} action in the symmetric form 𝒮g​[h→]=g​∑aha∗​Φa+h.c.\mathcal{S}_{g}[\vec{h}]=g\sum_{a}h_{a}^{*}\Phi_{a}+\mathrm{h.c.} with non-zero ha=i​sa​|𝒌a|​uah_{a}=\mathrm{i}s_{a}|{\bm{k}}_{a}|\,u_{a} for a=1,2,3a=1,2,3. From power-counting at the fixed point, we find a strong-coupling action that is scale-invariant and compatible with the symmetries at the fixed point as

𝒮sc​[h→]=−(2​cscχ)​|g​h→|χ\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{sc}}[\vec{h}]=-\left(\frac{2c_{\mathrm{sc}}}{\chi}\right)|g\,\vec{h}|^{\chi} (33)

with χ=3/(3−ΔΦ)>0\chi=3/(3-\Delta_{\Phi})>0 and csc>0c_{\mathrm{sc}}>0 an undetermined positive scaling constant [79]. This implies that in the scaling regime, we can write the deformation-induced change in the energy density as

Δ​ℰQED3​[𝒖]≡ℰQED3​[𝒖]−ℰQED3≈−2​cscχ​|g​|𝒌a||χ​|u→|χ.\Delta\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}[{\bm{u}}]\equiv\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}[{\bm{u}}]-\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}\approx-\frac{2c_{\mathrm{sc}}}{\chi}\big|g|{\bm{k}}_{a}|\big|^{\chi}|\vec{u}|^{\chi}. (34)

This non-analytic contribution to the ground-state energy must outcompete the (leading) quadratic energy cost for the longitudinal displacements, ℋph=κ​|u→|2\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{ph}}=\kappa|\vec{u}|^{2}. Comparing with Eq. (34), we find that it is energetically preferable for the system to undergo a lattice distortion with amplitude |u→|≠0|\vec{u}|\neq 0 as long as 0<χ<20<\chi<2. This implies that the instability occurs for monopole scaling dimensions ΔΦ<3/2\Delta_{\Phi}<3/2, which is satisfied by the assumed value ΔΦ≈1.02\Delta_{\Phi}\approx 1.02 [37].

Within this scaling ansatz, we can further estimate the magnitude of the induced displacement field by minimizing ℋph+Δ​ℰQED3​[𝒖]\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{ph}}+\Delta\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}[{\bm{u}}] with respect to |u→||\vec{u}|, and obtain

|u→|=|2​cscκ|3−ΔΦ3−2​ΔΦ​(g​|𝒌a|)33−2​ΔΦ.|\vec{u}|=\left|\frac{2c_{\mathrm{sc}}}{\kappa}\right|^{\frac{3-\Delta_{\Phi}}{3-2\Delta_{\Phi}}}\left(g|{\bm{k}}_{a}|\right)^{\frac{3}{3-2\Delta_{\Phi}}}. (35)

V.3 Symmetry of the distortion field

Both the perturbative approach in Sec. V.1 as well the scaling ansatz in Sec. V.2 suggest a weak-coupling instability of the Dirac spin liquid coupled to classical displacement fields. Importantly, the respective effective actions in Eqs. (30) and (34) were given as functions of the norm |u→||\vec{u}| of the complex vector u→=(u1,u2,u3)⊤\vec{u}=(u_{1},u_{2},u_{3})^{\top}, seemingly implying invariance under global G∈U⁡(3)G\in\mathrm{U}(3) transformations u^↦G​u^\hat{u}\mapsto G\hat{u}. However, this global continuous symmetry is accidental as it does not correspond to the physical symmetry group of microscopic lattice symmetries (consisting of translations, sixfold rotation C6C_{6} and mirror RR).

This accidental degeneracy has two distinct origins and thus will be lifted by two separate mechanisms. In the following, we argue that the resultant lattice distortion is C3C_{3} symmetric, and use this result to derive the microscopic form of the lattice distortion.

V.3.1 Lifting of accidental U⁡(3)\mathrm{U}(3) symmetry

We first note that aforementioned U⁡(3)\mathrm{U}(3) symmetry acts on the VBS monopoles, which transform as SO​(3)valley\mathrm{SO}(3)_{\mathrm{valley}}-vectors under the emergent symmetry group of the QED3\text{QED}_{3} fixed-point action. We therefore conclude that the global U⁡(3)\mathrm{U}(3) redundancy is an artifact of the approximations made to the effective action, in both the perturbative regime as well as using the scaling ansatz. To this end, we note that 2​𝒌1−2​𝒌2=2​𝒌2−2​𝒌3=2​𝒌1−2​𝒌3=02{\bm{k}}_{1}-2{\bm{k}}_{2}=2{\bm{k}}_{2}-2{\bm{k}}_{3}=2{\bm{k}}_{1}-2{\bm{k}}_{3}=0 up to reciprocal lattice vectors, and hence |h→⋅h→||\vec{h}\cdot\vec{h}| transforms trivially under the SO⁡(6)×U​(1)top\mathrm{SO}(6)\times\mathrm{U(1)}_{\mathrm{top}} symmetry group. This term will generically appear in an effective action obtained after ‘integrating out’ the Dirac spin liquid and breaks the U⁡(3)\mathrm{U}(3) redundancy down to SO​(3)valley\mathrm{SO(3)}_{\mathrm{valley}}. Importantly, we assume that these terms are small, so that they only act to select some states out of the accidentally-degenerate manifold, but not change the mangitude of the order parameter itself.

To be explicit, one may add a term ∼|h→⋅h→|χ/4\sim|\vec{h}\cdot\vec{h}|^{\chi/4} to the scaling form in Eq. (33), where we use again the short notation ha=i​sa​|𝒌a|​uah_{a}=\mathrm{i}s_{a}|{\bm{k}}_{a}|\,u_{a}. However, within the scaling ansatz, the sign of the coefficient of this term is left undetermined, such that the selected configuration may satisfy either h^⋅h^=0\hat{h}\cdot\hat{h}=0, or h^⋅h^=1\hat{h}\cdot\hat{h}=1 up to some phase (where h^=h→/|h→|\hat{h}=\vec{h}/|\vec{h}|). Within the perturbative regime on the other hand, we can identify terms at higher order in the lattice distortion field which leads to the following contribution to the ground state energy

ℰ(4)​[h→]∼|h→|4​(𝒞1​(β)+𝒞2​(β)​(h^⋅h^)​(h^∗⋅h^∗)),\mathcal{E}^{(4)}[\vec{h}]\sim|\vec{h}|^{4}\left(\mathcal{C}_{1}(\beta)+\mathcal{C}_{2}(\beta)\left(\hat{h}\cdot\hat{h}\right)\left(\hat{h}^{\ast}\cdot\hat{h}^{\ast}\right)\right), (36)

where 𝒞1​(β)\mathcal{C}_{1}(\beta) and 𝒞2​(β)\mathcal{C}_{2}(\beta) are some constants. This result is derived in Appendix C and comes from quadratic- and quartic-order in perturbation theory, considering all possible monopole- and fermion-lattice couplings. While the sign of 𝒞1​(β)\mathcal{C}_{1}(\beta) is a priori not determined, we find that the most dominant contribution to 𝒞2​(β)\mathcal{C}_{2}(\beta) is positive, from which we infer 𝒞2​(β)>0\mathcal{C}_{2}(\beta)>0 and thus the selected configuration will satisfy h^⋅h^=0\hat{h}\cdot\hat{h}=0.

V.3.2 Breaking of emergent SO⁡(3)\mathrm{SO}(3) symmetry in the ordered phase: Dangerously irrelevant operators

Under the constraint h^⋅h^≡0\hat{h}\cdot\hat{h}\equiv 0, it is easily seen that the effective actions (in both the perturbative regime and using the scaling ansatz) possess an SO​(3)valley\mathrm{SO(3)}_{\mathrm{valley}}-symmetry. A naive analysis might conclude that the spin-Peierls instability is concomitant with a spontaneous breaking of this continuous symmetry group, such that the resulting phase hosts Goldstone modes.

We now argue that this is not the case. We note that the SO​(3)valley⊂SO⁡(6)\mathrm{SO(3)}_{\mathrm{valley}}\subset\mathrm{SO}(6) is an emergent symmetry at the QED3 fixed point, which follows from the fact that there exist no relevant perturbations to the QED3 fixed point which are invariant under the microscopic (UV) symmetries of the system.

Crucially, the physics of the ordered state (i.e. after the system has undergone the spin-Peierls instability) is controlled by some new strong-coupling fixed point FP∗. This fixed point need not possess the same emergent symmetry; perturbations allowed by microscopic symmetries can constitute relevant perturbations to FP∗. This is the scenario of a dangerously irrelevant coupling λ\lambda [81, 82]. Initializing a renormalization-group (RG) flow in the vicinity of the QED3 (with finite λ,g≠0\lambda,g\neq 0), the relevant coupling gg will increase under the flow to FP∗, while the dangerously irrelevant λ\lambda initially decreases. Upon reaching some crossover scale, λ\lambda will start to grow as it constitutes a relevant perturbation to FP∗.

Specifically, as pointed out in Ref. [38], the DSL on the triangular lattice admits a three-monopole term

Sλ=λ∫d3x[Φ1Φ2Φ3+h.c.]S_{\lambda}=\lambda\int\mathrm{d}^{3}x\left[\Phi_{1}\Phi_{2}\Phi_{3}+\mathrm{h.c.}\right] (37)

which is allowed by the microscopic (UV) symmetries (for example, this three-monopole terms has zero lattice momentum since 𝒌1+𝒌2+𝒌3=0{\bm{k}}_{1}+{\bm{k}}_{2}+{\bm{k}}_{3}=0), but clearly breaks the emergent SO⁡(6)\mathrm{SO}(6) symmetry at the QED3 fixed point. Note that the three-monopole term has scaling dimension ΔΦ​Φ​Φ≈4.3\Delta_{\Phi\Phi\Phi}\approx 4.3 in the large-NN expansion and is therefore assumed to be irrelevant [36].

Considering the coupling of the DSL to displacement fields, any finite λ≠0\lambda\neq 0 induces analogous corresponding anharmonic terms in the effective action,

ℰλ[h→]∼λ~[h1h2h3+h.c.].\mathcal{E}_{\lambda}[\vec{h}]\sim\tilde{\lambda}\left[h_{1}h_{2}h_{3}+\mathrm{h.c.}\right]. (38)

Within perturbation theory about QED3\text{QED}_{3}, one contribution to the effective action of this form arises from ⟨Sg3​Sλ⟩/(β​V)\langle S^{3}_{g}S_{\lambda}\rangle/(\beta V). We stress that, since (38) is allowed by the microscopic symmetries of the system, it will also generically arise in any microscopic theory of lattice displacements upon going beyond the harmonic approximation, even in the absence of a coupling to the DSL (hence λ~\tilde{\lambda} is not necessarily related to λ\lambda in SλS_{\lambda}).

We hypothesize that the dynamics of the field h→\vec{h} at the strong-coupling fixed point may be described by an O(3) non-linear sigma model 11 1 Upcoming work [132]. This follows from the non-linear sigma model description of the Dirac spin liquid.. Then, any finite λ~\tilde{\lambda} gives rise to a finite mass term for the transverse Goldstone-mode fluctuations. We conclude that λ~≠0\tilde{\lambda}\neq 0 explicitly breaks the emergent SO​(3)valley\mathrm{SO(3)}_{\mathrm{valley}} symmetry of the model in the ordered phase. The resulting energy-minimizing configurations for λ~<0\tilde{\lambda}<0 are given by

h→GS=[u/3](1,e2​π​i/3,e−2πi/3)⊤.\vec{h}_{\mathrm{GS}}=[u/\sqrt{3}]\left(1,\mathrm{e}^{2\pi\mathrm{i}/3},\mathrm{e}^{-2\pi\mathrm{i}/3}\right)^{\top}. (39)

Instead of having a continuous SO⁡(3)\mathrm{SO(3)} manifold of degenerate ground states, there are three degenerate ground states e2​π​i​n/3​h→GS\mathrm{e}^{2\pi\mathrm{i}n/3}\vec{h}_{\mathrm{GS}}, with n=0,1,2n=0,1,2. The resultant lattice distortion preserves the C3=T1​C62C_{3}=T_{1}C_{6}^{2} lattice symmetry and has an additional reflection symmetry. In real-space, the pattern is written

𝒖⁡(𝒙)=2​Im⁡(∑asa​𝒌^a​hGSa​ei​𝒌a⋅𝒙),{\bm{u}}({\bm{x}})=2\operatorname{Im}\left(\sum_{a}s_{a}\hat{{\bm{k}}}_{a}\,h^{a}_{\mathrm{GS}}\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}{\bm{k}}_{a}\cdot{\bm{x}}}\right), (40)

which is highlighted in the left panel of Figure 1 with white arrows.

The spins react to the lattice breaking the translation and C6C_{6} rotation by forming a valence bond solid state with the same symmetries. In the field-theory picture, the choice of h→=h→GS\vec{h}=\vec{h}_{\mathrm{GS}} determines the ordering of the monopole excitations as g⁡⟨Φa⟩∼h^ag\langle\Phi_{a}\rangle\sim\hat{h}_{a}, up to a phase which we choose to be −1-1 (to minimize g⁡⟨Φa⟩​ha∗g\langle\Phi_{a}\rangle h_{a}^{*}). Using the mapping between VBS monopoles and nearest-neighbor spin dimer correlations Eq. (14), we can evaluate the predicted spin-spin correlation function

⟨S→𝒙⋅S→𝒙+𝜹a⟩=sa​Re⁡(⟨Φa⟩​ei​𝒌a⋅𝒙).\langle\vec{S}_{{\bm{x}}}\cdot\vec{S}_{{\bm{x}}+{\bm{\delta}}_{a}}\rangle=s_{a}\,\operatorname{Re}\left(\langle\Phi_{a}\rangle\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}{\bm{k}}_{a}\cdot{\bm{x}}}\right). (41)

This result is correct up to a normalization which symmetry arguments cannot determine. The resultant VBS order is plotted in Fig. 3. It has the strongest correlations at the boundary of the 12-site unit cell, and has negative dimer correlations on all bonds shortened by the lattice distortion — this is highlighted in Fig. 1. This pattern is related to the 12×12\sqrt{12}\times\sqrt{12} VBS patterns discussed in Refs. [38, 84, 85]; it is potentially generated by resonating, degenerate coverings of the enhanced bonds within the same 12-site unit cell.

VI Numerical study

We now turn to a numerical study of the triangular lattice J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} Heisenberg model, where simulations indicate the presence of a Dirac spin liquid ground state around J2/J1≈1/8J_{2}/J_{1}\approx 1/8 [30, 32, 49, 33]. We use the infinite density matrix renormalization group algorithm (DMRG) [46, 86, 48, 87] to study the lattice model on a cylinder of finite circumference Ly≡LL_{y}\equiv L [88, 89] and infinite length LxL_{x}. This limits the scope of the simulation by the introduction of a finite-size gap to the gapless DSL, but we will find that strong signatures of the DSL response remain, as seen in a previous study of the dynamical structure factor on a cylindrical geometry [49, 33].

VI.1 Finite geometries

Our theoretical CFT study predicts that the DSL has a strong energy response to a static distortion of the lattice with any of the three momenta 𝒌a{\bm{k}}_{a}. In the perturbative ‘weak coupling’ regime in the thermodynamic limit, this was found to be ∼−g2​|𝒌a|2​β3−2​ΔΦ​|u→|2\sim-g^{2}|{\bm{k}}_{a}|^{2}\beta^{3-2\Delta_{\Phi}}|\vec{u}|^{2}. At zero temperature, this quadratic contribution has a divergent prefactor; we expect that even in simulations for a finite system (meaning on cylinders with a finite circumference that cuts off our divergences), there will be a strong energy gain from a static lattice distortion with momenta 𝒌a{\bm{k}}_{a}. The spin-Peierls instability is recovered only in the thermodynamic limit. For any finite system circumference (smaller than the correlation length), the system’s energy will be an analytic function in the spin-Peierls coupling gg, and the change in energy Δ​ℰQED3​[u→]=ℰQED3​[u→]−ℰQED3​[0]\Delta\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}[\vec{u}]=\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}[\vec{u}]-\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}[0] due to coupling to a distortion field can be obtained using the perturbative expansion introduced in Sec. V.1,

ΔℰQED3[u→]=−limβ→∞12​β​V⟨Sg2⟩QED3+…,\Delta\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}[\vec{u}]=-\lim_{\beta\to\infty}\frac{1}{2\beta V}\langle S_{g}^{2}\rangle_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}+\dots, (42)

where ⟨Sg2⟩QED3\langle S_{g}^{2}\rangle_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}} can be obtained in an analogous manner to (29), but now performing the space-time integral on the geometry limβ→∞Sβ1×SL2\lim_{\beta\to\infty}S_{\beta}^{1}\times S_{L}^{2}, such that

Δ​ℰQED3​[u→]=c~ΔΦ​g2​|𝒌a|2​L3−2​ΔΦ​|u→|2\Delta\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}[\vec{u}]=\tilde{c}_{\Delta_{\Phi}}g^{2}|{\bm{k}}_{a}|^{2}\,L^{3-2\Delta_{\Phi}}|\vec{u}|^{2} (43)

where the constant c~ΔΦ=2​π3/2​Γ​(ΔΦ−1/2)/[(3−2​ΔΦ)​Γ​(ΔΦ)]\tilde{c}_{\Delta_{\Phi}}=2\pi^{3/2}{\Gamma(\Delta_{\Phi}-1/2)}/[{(3-2\Delta_{\Phi})\Gamma(\Delta_{\Phi})}]. For the small systems that can be simulated numerically, we expect to be in the weak-coupling regime, defined in the new regularization scheme as g2​|𝒌a|2​L3−2​ΔΦ​|u→|≪1g^{2}|{\bm{k}}_{a}|^{2}L^{3-2\Delta_{\Phi}}|\vec{u}|\ll 1. We conclude that deforming the critical QED3 theory with the relevant coupling gg to a distortion field at momenta 𝒌a{\bm{k}}_{a} induces a quadratic term in gg. Crucially, the power-law scaling of the finite-size dependent prefactor is determined by the scaling dimension of the relevant monopole operators [90].

In contrast, we expect that distortions at other momenta, e.g., the 𝑲{\bm{K}} or 𝑴{\bm{M}} points, will generically produce a finite response independent of system size. The corresponding energy gain for these patterns may also be calculated within perturbation theory but will produce a finite contribution to ⟨Sg⟩2\langle S_{g}\rangle^{2} due to the finite momentum-transfer (as for the terms with 𝑸≠−𝒌a{\bm{Q}}\neq-{\bm{k}}_{a} in Eq. (28)). We aim to provide supporting numerical evidence for our analytical results with a study of the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} triangular lattice in the DSL phase by demonstrating a response consistent with an instability in the thermodynamic limit, predicted above. A response which grows as L→∞L\to\infty will eventually lead to the breakdown of the weak-coupling regime for smaller |u→||\vec{u}|; in the thermodynamic limit the system will have a non-analytic behavior |u→|χ|\vec{u}|^{\chi} for all distortions and consequently realize the zero-coupling spin-Peierls instability. Although behaviour in the thermodynamic limit is impossible to extract from such finite-size simulations, we can use a preliminary finite-size scaling scheme to confirm compatibility with a divergent response for specific distortion patterns.

VI.2 DMRG simulation

Considering microscopic models, a lattice distortion couples to spins by a nearest-neighbor bond-length-dependent exchange, as shown by a mapping from monopoles to nearest-neighbour spin exchanges in Eq. (18). To compare the effect of several different static distortions on the ground state, we take a simple model for the variation of the exchange parameters on the triangular lattice Heisenberg model for different distortion patterns. Namely, we consider a lattice distortion 𝒖i{\bm{u}}_{i} which is periodic in a larger unit cell and then calculate the new nearest- and next-nearest-neighbor lengths 𝒓i​j=𝑹i​j+𝒖i​j{\bm{r}}_{ij}={\bm{R}}_{ij}+{\bm{u}}_{ij} (where 𝒖i​j=𝒖i−𝒖j{\bm{u}}_{ij}={\bm{u}}_{i}-{\bm{u}}_{j}). By assuming that all spin exchange couplings Ji​jJ_{ij} are independent of bond angle, and exponentially dependent on the bond lengths Ji​j=J(0)​e−α​|𝒓i​j|J_{ij}=J^{(0)}\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha|{\bm{r}}_{ij}|} (where J(0)=J1,2J^{(0)}=J_{1,2} for NN/NNN couplings), we derive the leading contribution for small distortion

Ji​j=J(0)​[1−α​𝒖i​j⋅𝑹i​j/|𝑹i​j|].J_{ij}=J^{(0)}\left[1-\alpha\,{\bm{u}}_{ij}\cdot{\bm{R}}_{ij}/|{\bm{R}}_{ij}|\right]. (44)

Hereon, we absorb the dimensionful prefactor α\alpha into the distortion 𝜹i​j=α​𝒖i​j{\bm{\delta}}_{ij}=\alpha\,{\bm{u}}_{ij}, and think of distortions where |𝜹i​j|≪1|{\bm{\delta}}_{ij}|\ll 1. For the C3C_{3} symmetric pattern, the bond-strengths are highlighted in the left panel of Fig. 1. For all simulations presented in this work, we considered a ratio of (undistorted) nearest to next-nearest neighbour coupling of J2J1=1/8\frac{J_{2}}{J_{1}}=1/8, which lies within the regime of the putative Dirac quantum spin liquid phase [91, 49, 33].

VI.2.1 Energy response to distortion

We will now compare the response of four patterns: the three-site distortion with momentum −𝑲3-{\bm{K}}_{3}, the two-site distortions for momenta 𝑴i{\bm{M}}_{i} (i=1,2,3i=1,2,3), the six-site distortion 𝒌3=−𝑲3/2{\bm{k}}_{3}=-{\bm{K}}_{3}/2, and the 12-site pattern comprised of all 𝒌a=1,2,3{\bm{k}}_{a=1,2,3} [this distortion pattern is plotted in Fig. 4(b)]. We predict that this C3C_{3} symmetric pattern, defined in real-space by Eq. (40), will show the strongest response. The patterns given in terms of a single momentum eigenstate 𝑸=−𝑲3,𝑴i,𝒌3{\bm{Q}}=-{\bm{K}}_{3},{\bm{M}}_{i},{\bm{k}}_{3} (i=1,2,3i=1,2,3) are given simply by 𝒖i=u⁡(cos⁡[𝑸⋅𝒙i+θ],sin⁡[𝑸⋅𝒙i+θ]){\bm{u}}_{i}=u(\cos[{\bm{Q}}\cdot{\bm{x}}_{i}+\theta],\sin[{\bm{Q}}\cdot{\bm{x}}_{i}+\theta]), where θ∈[0,2​π]\theta\in[0,2\pi] is an arbitrary but fixed phase. The detailed phases used are specified in Appendix D. In all cases, the states can be written as either one or a sum of three momentum eigenstates satisfying the normalization ∑𝒒|𝒖𝒒|2=u2\sum_{{\bm{q}}}|{\bm{u}}_{{\bm{q}}}|^{2}=u^{2}. The energy cost of all patterns is defined through Eq. (23), giving ℋ⁡[u]=𝒦𝑸​u2\mathcal{H}[u]=\mathcal{K}_{{\bm{Q}}}u^{2} with

𝒦𝑴=8​K3​𝖺2,𝒦𝑲=5​K3​𝖺2,κ=𝒦𝒌a=(5−2​3)​K3​𝖺2.\mathcal{K}_{{\bm{M}}}=\frac{8K}{3\mathsf{a}^{2}},\,\,\mathcal{K}_{{\bm{K}}}=\frac{5K}{3\mathsf{a}^{2}},\,\,\kappa=\mathcal{K}_{{\bm{k}}_{a}}=\frac{(5-2\sqrt{3})K}{3\mathsf{a}^{2}}. (45)

The patterns with larger unit cells have a generally smaller energy cost for the same momentum-space distortion magnitude u2u^{2}, meaning the 𝒌a{\bm{k}}_{a} patterns have the lowest potential energy cost of the patterns we will compare. Note that in simulations of a distorted Heisenberg model, we calculate the spin energy gain in terms of the dimensionless distortion parameter δ=α​u\delta=\alpha u, where the constant α\alpha is equal for all patterns. Whether or not a finite-size lattice will spontaneously and statically distort with a given pattern, is determined by the relative magnitudes of the energy gain and the potential energy cost ℋ⁡[δ]=(𝒦𝑸/α2−A𝑸)​δ2\mathcal{H}[\delta]=(\mathcal{K}_{{\bm{Q}}}/\alpha^{2}-A_{{\bm{Q}}})\,\delta^{2}, where A𝑸A_{{\bm{Q}}} is the coefficient of the energy gain of the spins, to be computed numerically.

To model the lattice distortion, we stabilize the spin-disordered ground state on a translationally invariant lattice (we take the J2=J1/8J_{2}=J_{1}/8 parameter value in the spin-liquid regime). We simulate a cylindrical geometry infinite in the xx-direction by repeating a Lx=3,6L_{x}=3,6 unit cell (chosen to be compatible with the distortion pattern). We consider first a cylinder with circumference Ly=6L_{y}=6 using the Y​C​6YC6 boundary conditions [92, 91] (see Appendix D for details). We then introduce a small distortion of the lattice according to one of the patterns, distort the NN and NNN bonds accordingly, and then use DMRG to find the ground state on the new lattice. We use the spin-disordered ground state as the starting run and make no assumptions about the resultant spin state. Increasing the distortion parameter δ\delta proceeds by increasing the lattice distortion and calculating the resultant ground state with its energy. This process is repeated for increasing bond dimension χ\chi (up to 40004000) in order to ensure the resultant energy differences are well converged. A detailed description of this method, as well as figures showing all distortion patterns investigated, is provided in Appendix D.

A comparison of the energy gain of the spins −Δ​ℰ​[δ]=ℰ⁡[0]−ℰ⁡[δ]-\Delta\mathcal{E}[\delta]=\mathcal{E}[0]-\mathcal{E}[\delta] in the presence of three lattice distortions on the Ly=6L_{y}=6 cylinder are shown in Figure 4. We model the energy gain as −Δ​ℰ​[δ]=A𝑸​δα-\Delta\mathcal{E}[\delta]=A_{{\bm{Q}}}\delta^{\alpha} and use this form to fit the data. All curves are consistent with a quadratic response at small distortions, and we can see that the 12-site unit cell pattern has a much stronger response amplitude. The coupling of the DSL to a lattice distortion commensurate with the monopole excitations leads to the strongest response. We also note that the symmetric combination of all three momenta 𝒌a{\bm{k}}_{a} leads to a stronger response than 𝒌3{\bm{k}}_{3} individually, as predicted in Section V.3. An analysis of the convergence of the DMRG calculations, as well as the results of the fitting performed with logarithmic axes is provided in Appendix D. We conclude that at this bond dimension, the change in energy due to distortion is well converged on Ly=6L_{y}=6 geometries.

VI.2.2 VBS order

Now we turn to the VBS order on the deformed lattices. In Fig. 4(c), the nearest-neighbor spin-spin correlations ⟨S→⋅S→⟩\langle\vec{S}\cdot\vec{S}\rangle of the symmetric 12-site patterns are plotted and compared to the uniform correlations of the DSL ground state in the undistorted model. The correlations shown have been obtained for bond dimension χ=2000\chi=2000 after adiabatically increasing the distortion δ\delta. The undistorted ground state had been optimized using the odd-sector method for the same bond dimension (see Appendix D for details). It matches well with our prediction of the condensation of three monopoles ⟨Φa⟩∼e2​π​i​a/3\langle\Phi_{a}\rangle\sim\mathrm{e}^{2\pi\mathrm{i}\,a/3} (cf. Fig. 3), showing strong negative VBS weight (relative to the DSL) on the boundaries of the 12-site unit cell (particularly on the shorter sides, which we observe are stronger than the central triangle). Importantly, the more negative VBS weights are inside the unit cell along bonds that are shortened by the distortion, and we additionally see a more positive weight between the unit cells along lengthened bonds. The large variation of bond order (up to range ≈0.4\approx 0.4) in the VBS state is significantly larger than the almost uniform DSL state, with correlations −0.181-0.181 and variations of order 10−310^{-3}. This variation in dimer correlations serves as a VBS order parameter and is a clear sign here of the transition away from the DSL. We have hence seen that the 12-site lattice distortion leads to a strong energetic gain and transition to a short-range correlated phase, which is consistent with a DSL-VBS transition on a finite-circumference cylinder.

VI.2.3 System-size dependence

Next, we test the prediction of the weak-coupling CFT calculation and connect to the thermodynamic limit by performing finite-size scaling. We will show that the magnitude of the energy response as a function of system size A𝑸​(L)A_{{\bm{Q}}}(L) is only non-trivial for the static distortions that couple to monopoles.

We consider finite-size systems with circumference Ly=3,6,9L_{y}=3,6,9; since the symmetric pattern cannot fit on these new geometries, we are restricted to only studying the momentum-eigenstate patterns 𝑸=𝑴3,𝑲3,𝒌3{\bm{Q}}={\bm{M}}_{3},{\bm{K}}_{3},{\bm{k}}_{3}. These patterns all fit in a six-site unit cell, which we can fit on the YC​N\mathrm{YC}N geometry for NN a multiple of 3.

The responses for the three patterns with bond dimension up to χ=7000\chi=7000 are plotted in Figure 5. The responses Δ​E​(δ)\Delta E(\delta) for L=3,6L=3,6 are well converged for all δ\delta and well described by a quadratic response α=2\alpha=2; for L=9L=9, we are able to converge one point δ=0.02\delta=0.02 for the three patterns. Due to this numerical limitation, we cannot compare the amplitudes obtained from fitting for all system sizes, so instead we focus on comparing the energy gain Δ​E​(δ=0.002)\Delta E(\delta=0.002) in the inset as a function of system size. We find that only the monopole pattern with 𝒌3{\bm{k}}_{3} shows significant system-size dependence, with its amplitude increasing strongly. In contrast, the 𝑲3{\bm{K}}_{3} response amplitude does not significantly increase, and the 𝑴3{\bm{M}}_{3} response even slightly reduces in amplitude. This difference of behavior under variation of cylinder circumference seems to confirm that the system is unstable to only lattice distortions with momenta 𝒌a{\bm{k}}_{a} in the thermodynamic limit. We conclude that the numerical simulations, even though performed on small cylinder circumferences, are compatible with our prediction of a zero-coupling instability in the thermodynamic limit.

VII Dynamical phonons

In the derivation of the weak-coupling spin-Peierls instability, we made the crucial assumption that the lattice displacements can be treated as a classical background field without any intrinsic dynamics. This adiabatic approximation is justified if the magnetic energy scales (such as bare microscopic exchange couplings) are much larger than those of the lattice displacements, such that the lattice dynamics occurs on much longer time scales compared to the spin subsystem. In the case of the one-dimensional spin-Peierls transition, the treatment of dynamical phonons removes the zero-coupling instability and produces a stable spin-liquid regime [67].

In this section, we go beyond the adiabatic assumption for the DSL.
