To this end, we focus on the relevant interaction between valley-triplet monopoles and lattice distortions at wavevectors 𝒌a{\bm{k}}_{a} with a=1,2,3a=1,2,3 and now promote the corresponding Fourier components to dynamical fields 𝒖𝒌a→𝒖𝒌a​(τ,𝒙){\bm{u}}_{{\bm{k}}_{a}}\to{\bm{u}}_{{\bm{k}}_{a}}(\tau,{\bm{x}}).

VII.1 Integrating out dynamical phonons

We add dynamics for the long-wavelength fluctuations of the 𝒌a{\bm{k}}_{a}-displacement modes via a (heuristic) kinetic energy term, 𝒮kin=ρ​∑a|∂τua​(𝒙,τ)|2\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{kin}}=\rho\sum_{a}|\partial_{\tau}u_{a}({\bm{x}},\tau)|^{2}, where we directly work in terms of the longitudinal components ua=𝒌^a⋅𝒖𝒌au_{a}=\hat{{\bm{k}}}_{a}\cdot{\bm{u}}_{{\bm{k}}_{a}} and ρ\rho corresponds to a microscopic mass density of phonon degrees of freedom. The lattice stiffness is given as before by κ∼K/𝖺2\kappa\sim K/\mathsf{a}^{2}, but is now taken to be independent of momentum. Here, ua​(τ,𝒙)u_{a}(\tau,{\bm{x}}) is to be understood as a complex scalar field, since the Fourier components 𝒖𝒌a=𝒖−𝒌a∗{\bm{u}}_{{\bm{k}}_{a}}={\bm{u}}_{-{\bm{k}}_{a}}^{\ast}. The full (dynamical) action then reads

Sph​[ua]=∫d​τ​∫d2​𝒙​[ρ​|∂τua​(τ,𝒙)|2+κ​|ua​(τ,𝒙)|2].S_{\mathrm{ph}}[u_{a}]=\int\!\mathrm{d}\tau\!\int\!\mathrm{d}^{2}{\bm{x}}\left[\rho|\partial_{\tau}u_{a}(\tau,{\bm{x}})|^{2}+\kappa|u_{a}(\tau,{\bm{x}})|^{2}\right]. (46)

Note that for simplicity we have not included gradient terms which would induce a long-wavelength dispersion for the ua​(𝒙,τ)u_{a}({\bm{x}},\tau)-fields, since SphS_{\mathrm{ph}} already includes an explicit energy gap ω0≡κ/ρ\omega_{0}\equiv\sqrt{\kappa/\rho} for the phonons. Writing ua​(τ)=(2​π)−1​∫d​ω​e−i​ω​τ​ua​(ω)u_{a}(\tau)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int\mathrm{d}\omega\,\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\omega\tau}u_{a}(\omega) and Fourier-transforming G⁡(ω)=(ρ​ω2+κ)−1G(\omega)=(\rho\omega^{2}+\kappa)^{-1}, we find the phonon Green’s function from Eq. (46) as

⟨ua​(x)​ub∗​(y)⟩ph=δa,b​G​(x−y)=δa,b​δ(2)​(𝒙−𝒚)2​ρ​ω0​e−ω0​|τx−τy|,\langle u_{a}(x)u_{b}^{\ast}(y)\rangle_{\mathrm{ph}}=\delta_{a,b}G(x-y)=\delta_{a,b}\frac{\delta^{(2)}({\bm{x}}-{\bm{y}})}{2\rho\omega_{0}}\mathrm{e}^{-\omega_{0}|\tau_{x}-\tau_{y}|}, (47)

again with the short notation x=(τ,𝒙)x=(\tau,{\bm{x}}). The Green’s function G⁡(x−y)G(x-y) simply corresponds to a local imaginary-time Green’s function of a harmonic oscillator.

The full action SS of the system then reads

S⁡[ua​(τ,𝒙)]=Sph​[ua​(τ,𝒙)]+SQED3+Sg,S[u_{a}(\tau,{\bm{x}})]=S_{\mathrm{ph}}[u_{a}(\tau,{\bm{x}})]+S_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}+S_{g}, (48)

where SQED3S_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}} is the fixed-point action for QED3, and Sg=∫d​τ​d2​𝒙​ℋgS_{g}=\int\mathrm{d}\tau\mathrm{d}^{2}{\bm{x}}\,\mathcal{H}_{g} is the coupling between monopoles and (now dynamical) phonons, see Eq. (21). Crucially, as long as the phonons remain gapped ω0>0\omega_{0}>0, these degrees of freedom can be integrated out exactly (owing to their quadratic, non-interacting nature) to obtain an effective action for the QED3\text{QED}_{3} degrees of freedom. Explicitly, using the equation of motion

ua​(x)=(i​|𝒌a|​g​sa)​∫d3​y​G​(x−y)​Φa​(y)u_{a}(x)=\big(\mathrm{i}|{\bm{k}}_{a}|gs_{a}\big)\int\mathrm{d}^{3}y\,G(x-y)\Phi_{a}(y) (49)

we find the system’s full action S=SQED3+SΦ​ΦS=S_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}+S_{\Phi\Phi} where integrating out the dynamical phonon degrees of freedom induces an effective interaction among the monopole operators,

SΦ​Φ=−g2∑a|𝒌a|2∫d3xd3yΦa†(x)G(x−y)Φa(y).S_{\Phi\Phi}=-g^{2}\sum_{a}|{\bm{k}}_{a}|^{2}\int\mathrm{d}^{3}x\,\mathrm{d}^{3}y\ \Phi_{a}^{\dagger}(x)G(x-y)\Phi_{a}(y). (50)

We note that the monopole-monopole interaction in (50) is local in space but retarded in time.

VII.2 Phase transition at finite frequencies

In the adiabatic limit ω0=0\omega_{0}=0 the monopole-monopole interaction in (50) becomes non-local in time. This implies that modes become correlated at large (temporal) separations, leading to an ordering instability at infinitesimal couplings as per the results of Sec. V. Continuing to finite frequencies ω0>0\omega_{0}>0, one may be tempted to perform a mean-field decoupling of the monopole-monopole interaction in SΦ​ΦS_{\Phi\Phi}. This would capture an ordering instability by some finite (and time-independent) monopole expectation value [79], Φ⁡(x)→⟨Φ⟩MF​(x)≠0\Phi(x)\to\langle\Phi\rangle_{\mathrm{MF}}(x)\neq 0. However, an explicit perturbative mean-field calculation (again employing an explicit IR regularization, e.g. by working at finite temperature) reveals a criticality condition identical to the static case obtained in Sec. V.1.3, which crucially does not depend on ω0\omega_{0}. This is understood to be an artifact of mean-field theory which neglects the retardation of the monopole-monopole interaction in SΦ​ΦS_{\Phi\Phi}, and thus cannot capture any effects due to having non-zero phonon frequency ω0\omega_{0}. This may also be seen explicitly: After decoupling, (schematic notation) Φ†​Φ→⟨Φ†⟩MF​Φ+Φ†​⟨Φ⟩MF−⟨Φ†⟩MF​⟨Φ⟩MF\Phi^{\dagger}\Phi\to\langle\Phi^{\dagger}\rangle_{\mathrm{MF}}\Phi+\Phi^{\dagger}\langle\Phi\rangle_{\mathrm{MF}}-\langle\Phi^{\dagger}\rangle_{\mathrm{MF}}\langle\Phi\rangle_{\mathrm{MF}}, with time-independent ⟨Φ⟩MF\langle\Phi\rangle_{\mathrm{MF}}, the effective action becomes equivalent to the classical action ℋph+ℋg​[𝒖]+𝒮QED3\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{ph}}+\mathcal{H}_{g}[{\bm{u}}]+\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}} considered in Sec. V, if one relates the monopole mean-field expectation value to an effective displacement field.

In the opposite, antiadiabatic, limit ω0→∞\omega_{0}\rightarrow\infty (with κ\kappa constant), the Green’s function becomes purely local, G⁡(x−y)=(1/2​ρ)​δ(3)​(x−y)G(x-y)=(1/2\rho)\,\delta^{(3)}(x-y). Note that in this limit, the monopole-monopole interaction becomes singular due to the OPE limϵ−>0Φ†​(ϵ+x)​Φ​(x)∼𝟙/ϵ2​ΔΦ\lim_{\epsilon->0}\Phi^{\dagger}(\epsilon+x)\Phi(x)\sim\mathds{1}/\epsilon^{2\Delta_{\Phi}}. To regularize this, one may work with a finite UV cutoff a≤|x−y|a\leq|x-y| that enforces a lower bound on the monopole-monopole separation. Then, upon taking ω0→∞\omega_{0}\to\infty at some fixed cutoff, the interaction effectively vanishes and the DSL remains stable. Considering both limits, it becomes clear that there must exist some transition at some intermediate coupling gg determined by ω0\omega_{0}.

To obtain the critical interaction strength as a function of ω0\omega_{0}, we perform a scaling analysis using the exponential form of G⁡(τx−τy)G(\tau_{x}-\tau_{y}) in Eq. (47): For separations |τx−τy|≳1/ω0|\tau_{x}-\tau_{y}|\gtrsim 1/\omega_{0}, the interaction is exponentially suppressed, thereby setting a critical cutoff scale ac∼1/ω0a_{c}\sim 1/\omega_{0}. Starting with some cutoff a<aca<a_{c}, we can increase the cutoff up to aca_{c} where the interaction becomes suppressed. Rescaling all coordinates x=x′/acx=x^{\prime}/a_{c} (with x′x^{\prime} now dimensionless) reveals the critical (dimensionless) interaction scale 1∼g2​ω2​ΔΦ−3/(𝖺2​κ)1\sim g^{2}\omega^{2\Delta_{\Phi}-3}/(\mathsf{a}^{2}\kappa), or equivalently gc2∼κ​𝖺2​ω03−2​Δg_{c}^{2}\sim\kappa\mathsf{a}^{2}\omega_{0}^{3-2\Delta} (where we use that |𝒌|∼1/𝖺|{\bm{k}}|\sim 1/\mathsf{a} with 𝖺\mathsf{a} being the lattice spacing).

VII.3 Perturbation theory

We now investigate the stability of the DSL in the presence of the interaction SΦ​ΦS_{\Phi\Phi} within perturbation theory. Considering a perturbative expansion of local observables, the expansion’s breakdown is taken to signal an instability of the DSL. We employ the path-integral formalism, where the expectation value of some observable 𝒳\mathcal{X} is written as ⟨𝒳⟩=𝒵−1​∫𝒟⁡[{𝒪CFT}]​𝒳​e−S\langle\mathcal{X}\rangle=\mathcal{Z}^{-1}\int\mathcal{D}[\{\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{CFT}}\}]\,\mathcal{X}\mathrm{e}^{-S} where SS is the system’s interacting action and 𝒵\mathcal{Z} its partition function without operator insertion, as above.

At the QED3 fixed point (i.e. zeroth order perturbation theory), all one-point functions vanish at zero temperature β→∞\beta\to\infty in the thermodynamic limit by conformal symmetry. We thus turn to the monopole two-point function at large distances |d|=|(𝒅,τd)|→∞|d|=|({\bm{d}},\tau_{d})|\to\infty. Expanding the Boltzmann weight e−SΦ​Φ\mathrm{e}^{-S_{\Phi\Phi}} in the path integral to first order, one finds the perturbative expansion

⟨Φa†​(d)​Φb​(0)⟩g2=δa​b|d|2​ΔΦ−(⟨Φa†​(d)​Φb​(0)​SΦ​Φ⟩QED3−δa​b|d|2​ΔΦ​⟨SΦ​Φ⟩QED3)+…,\langle\Phi^{\dagger}_{a}(d)\Phi_{b}(0)\rangle_{g^{2}}=\frac{\delta_{ab}}{|d|^{2\Delta_{\Phi}}}\\ -\left(\langle\Phi^{\dagger}_{a}(d)\Phi_{b}(0)S_{\Phi\Phi}\rangle_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}-\frac{\delta_{ab}}{|d|^{2\Delta_{\Phi}}}\langle S_{\Phi\Phi}\rangle_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}\right)+\dots, (51)

where we have used Eq. (13) for two-point functions evaluated at the CFT fixed point. The first term in the parenthesis is written explicitly as

⟨Φa†(d)Φb(0)SΦ​Φ⟩QED3=−∑cg2​|𝒌c|22​ρ​ω0∫d3xd3y[δ(2)(𝒙−𝒚)e−ω0​|τx−τy|⟨Φa†(d)Φb(0)Φc†(x)Φc(y)⟩QED3].\langle\Phi^{\dagger}_{a}(d)\Phi_{b}(0)S_{\Phi\Phi}\rangle_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}=-\sum_{c}\frac{g^{2}|{\bm{k}}_{c}|^{2}}{2\rho\omega_{0}}\int\mathrm{d}^{3}x\mathrm{d}^{3}y\left[\delta^{(2)}({\bm{x}}-{\bm{y}})\mathrm{e}^{-\omega_{0}|\tau_{x}-\tau_{y}|}\langle\Phi^{\dagger}_{a}(d)\Phi_{b}(0)\Phi^{\dagger}_{c}(x)\Phi_{c}(y)\rangle_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}\right]. (52)

Note that while 2- and 3-pt. functions of primaries are exactly determined by conformal symmetry, no closed forms are available for 4-pt. functions, making the evaluation of Eq. (51) challenging.

While Wick’s theorem does not hold in interacting CFT, we can successively apply operator product expansions (OPE) to decompose the 4-pt. function in (52). If the full (convergent) OPE is used, the choice of OPE channels is inconsequential (indeed, demanding OPE associativity lies at the heart of CFT bootstrap studies [93]). However, for analytical tractability, we will use the asymptotic forms of OPE [see also Eq. (68)]. A particular OPE channel then corresponds to a particular configuration of operator insertions which yield the most divergent contribution in the particular channel if they become ‘close’.

Considering Eq. (52), we will focus on the leading monopole-antimonopole OPE channel (schematically Φ†×Φ=𝟙\Phi^{\dagger}\times\Phi=\mathds{1}) corresponding to x→0x\to 0 and y→dy\to d, with xx and yy sufficiently far apart, which means that we may assume 0<|x|≪|y|0<|x|\ll|y|. Explicitly, the first-order OPE in this channel then reads

⟨Φa†​(d)​Φb​(0)​Φc†​(x)​Φc​(y)⟩QED3∼δa​c​δb​c​1|d−y|2​ΔΦ​|x|2​ΔΦ.\langle\Phi^{\dagger}_{a}(d)\Phi_{b}(0)\Phi^{\dagger}_{c}(x)\Phi_{c}(y)\rangle_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}\sim\delta_{ac}\delta_{bc}\frac{1}{|d-y|^{2\Delta_{\Phi}}|x|^{2\Delta_{\Phi}}}. (53)

We expect this channel to give the most dominant contribution: The other monopole-antimonopole channel corresponding to d→0d\to 0, x→yx\to y is asymptotically equivalent to the disconnected contribution (second term in the parenthesis) in Eq. (52), and is thus expected to only weakly contribute to ⟨Φa†​(d)​Φb​(0)⟩g2\langle\Phi^{\dagger}_{a}(d)\Phi_{b}(0)\rangle_{g^{2}}.

We use (53) in (52). As |d|→∞|d|\to\infty, we can take |d−y|−2​ΔΦ≈|d|−2​ΔΦ|d-y|^{-2\Delta_{\Phi}}\approx|d|^{-2\Delta_{\Phi}} and subsequently perform the 𝒚{\bm{y}}-integration, yielding

⟨Φa†​(d)​Φb​(0)​SΦ​Φ⟩QED3≈−δa​b|d|2​ΔΦg2​|𝒌a|22​ρ​ω0∫d3x∫dτye−ω0​|τx−τy|(|𝒙|2+τx2)ΔΦ.\langle\Phi^{\dagger}_{a}(d)\Phi_{b}(0)S_{\Phi\Phi}\rangle_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}\approx\\ -\frac{\delta_{ab}}{|d|^{2\Delta_{\Phi}}}\frac{g^{2}|{\bm{k}}_{a}|^{2}}{2\rho\omega_{0}}\int\mathrm{d}^{3}x\int\mathrm{d}\tau_{y}\,\frac{\mathrm{e}^{-\omega_{0}|\tau_{x}-\tau_{y}|}}{(|{\bm{x}}|^{2}+\tau_{x}^{2})^{\Delta_{\Phi}}}. (54)

We work on a cylindrical geometry Sβ1×ℝ2​→β→∞​ℝ3S_{\beta}^{1}\times\mathbb{R}^{2}\overset{\beta\to\infty}{\to}\mathbb{R}^{3}. The spatial integration is performed in polar coordinates with 0<|𝒙|<L→∞0<|{\bm{x}}|<L\to\infty,

|d|2​ΔΦ​⟨Φa†​(d)​Φb​(0)​SΦ​Φ⟩QED3≈−δa​bπ​g2​|𝒌a|22​(ΔΦ−1)​ρ​ω0∫dτxdτye−ω0​|τx−τy||τx|2​ΔΦ−2.|d|^{2\Delta_{\Phi}}\langle\Phi^{\dagger}_{a}(d)\Phi_{b}(0)S_{\Phi\Phi}\rangle_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}\approx\\ -\delta_{ab}\frac{\pi g^{2}|{\bm{k}}_{a}|^{2}}{2(\Delta_{\Phi}-1)\rho\omega_{0}}\int\mathrm{d}\tau_{x}\mathrm{d}\tau_{y}\,\frac{\mathrm{e}^{-\omega_{0}|\tau_{x}-\tau_{y}|}}{|\tau_{x}|^{2\Delta_{\Phi}-2}}. (55)

Note that due to the δ\delta-distribution for the spatial components in (52), only configurations with 𝒙=𝒚{\bm{x}}={\bm{y}} give a finite contribution. Thus, our previous assumption of |x|≪|y||x|\ll|y| implies for the temporal coordinates |τx|≪|τy||\tau_{x}|\ll|\tau_{y}|. With |τx−τy|≈|τy||\tau_{x}-\tau_{y}|\approx|\tau_{y}|, the remaining integrals are obtained as

limβ→∞∫0βd​τy​∫0|τy|d​τx​e−ω0​|τy||τx|2​ΔΦ−2≈13−2​ΔΦ​Γ⁡(4−2​ΔΦ)ω04−2​ΔΦ,\lim_{\beta\to\infty}\int_{0}^{\beta}\mathrm{d}\tau_{y}\int_{0}^{|\tau_{y}|}\mathrm{d}\tau_{x}\,\frac{\mathrm{e}^{-\omega_{0}|\tau_{y}|}}{|\tau_{x}|^{2\Delta_{\Phi}-2}}\approx\frac{1}{3-2\Delta_{\Phi}}\frac{\Gamma(4-2\Delta_{\Phi})}{\omega_{0}^{4-2\Delta_{\Phi}}}, (56)

which exists for ΔΦ<2\Delta_{\Phi}<2, which is within the range of assumed scaling dimensions. Hence, one finds

|d|2​ΔΦ​⟨Φa†​(d)​Φb​(0)​SΦ​Φ⟩QED3≈−δa​b​cΔΦ​Γ​(4−2​ΔΦ)4​ρ​ω02​g2​|𝒌a|2ω03−2​ΔΦ|d|^{2\Delta_{\Phi}}\langle\Phi^{\dagger}_{a}(d)\Phi_{b}(0)S_{\Phi\Phi}\rangle_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}\approx-\delta_{ab}\frac{c_{\Delta_{\Phi}}\Gamma(4-2\Delta_{\Phi})}{4\rho\omega_{0}^{2}}\frac{g^{2}|{\bm{k}}_{a}|^{2}}{\omega_{0}^{3-2\Delta_{\Phi}}} (57)

Generically, perturbation theory breaks down when the (n+1)(n+1)-term in the expansion is no longer small compared to the nn-th term. Here, we compare the first-order correction to the bare correlator,

δ(1)​⟨Φa†​(d)​Φa​(0)⟩g2⟨Φa†​(d)​Φa​(0)⟩QED3≈14​cΔΦ​Γ​(4−2​ΔΦ)​g2​|𝒌a|2κ​ω03−2​ΔΦ.\frac{\delta^{(1)}\langle\Phi_{a}^{\dagger}(d)\Phi_{a}(0)\rangle_{g^{2}}}{\langle\Phi_{a}^{\dagger}(d)\Phi_{a}(0)\rangle_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}}\approx\frac{1}{4}c_{\Delta_{\Phi}}\Gamma(4-2\Delta_{\Phi})\frac{g^{2}|{\bm{k}}_{a}|^{2}}{\kappa\omega_{0}^{3-2\Delta_{\Phi}}}. (58)

Perturbation theory breaks down if this ratio is of order 1. This leads to a scaling relation for the critical coupling, given by

gc2∼K​ω03−2​ΔΦ.g^{2}_{c}\sim K\omega_{0}^{3-2\Delta_{\Phi}}. (59)

In the thermodynamic limit at zero temperature, the finite phonon frequency ω0≠0\omega_{0}\neq 0 hence prevents a weak-coupling instability and rather determines a critical gcg_{c} as a function of ω0\omega_{0}. The critical gcg_{c} matches precisely the result of the scaling analysis in Sec. VII.2.

VII.4 Monopole-induced phonon softening and Kohn-type anomalies

While in the previous subsections we have integrated out the dynamical phonons and analyzed the resulting monopole-monopole interactions in the Dirac spin liquid, we here take the opposite route and investigate how the phonon-monopole coupling is manifested in spectral properties of the phonon. In particular, we conclude that there exists a Kohn-like anomaly [94, 95] in the phonon dispersion, i.e. at (and close to) the wavevectors 𝑲a/2{\bm{K}}_{a}/2 there will be a characteristic softening of the otherwise gapped (away from 𝒒≡0{\bm{q}}\equiv 0) phonon. This can be understood in analogoy to the Kohn anomaly due to the divergent particle-hole susceptibility at 2​kF2k_{\mathrm{F}} in 1+1-dim. systems [94, 95].

Working at second order perturbation theory, we find that (21) yields a correction to the propagator of the phonon mode with lattice momentum 𝑲a/2{\bm{K}}_{a}/2 [cf. Eq. (46)], given by

Ga−1​(ω)=ρ​ω2+κ−g2​|𝒌a|2​⟨Φa†​Φa⟩QED3​(ω).G^{-1}_{a}(\omega)=\rho\omega^{2}+\kappa-g^{2}|{\bm{k}}_{a}|^{2}\langle\Phi^{\dagger}_{a}\Phi_{a}\rangle_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}(\omega). (60)

Continuing to real frequencies, this implies that the phonon quasiparticle dispersion ωa\omega_{a} becomes renormalized and is determined by solutions to the implicit equation

ω2=ω02−g2​|𝒌a|2​ρ−1​χa′​(ω,T),\omega^{2}=\omega_{0}^{2}-{g^{2}|{\bm{k}}_{a}|^{2}}{\rho}^{-1}\chi_{a}^{\prime}(\omega,T), (61)

where χ′\chi^{\prime} is the real part of the (in general TT-dependent) VBS susceptibility χa′​(ω,T)≡Re⁡χVBS​(ω,𝒌a+δ​𝒒,T)|δ​𝒒=0\chi^{\prime}_{a}(\omega,T)\equiv\operatorname{Re}\chi_{\mathrm{VBS}}(\omega,{\bm{k}}_{a}+\delta{\bm{q}},T)|_{\delta{\bm{q}}=0}, which for momenta close to 𝒌a{\bm{k}}_{a} is given by singular VBS monopole-monopole correlations [41].

For temperatures T≫ωT\gg\omega, scaling arguments imply that to leading order χa′​(ω,T)∼T−(3−2​ΔΦ)​(c+𝒪⁡(ω/T))\chi_{a}^{\prime}(\omega,T)\sim T^{-(3-2\Delta_{\Phi})}\left(c+\mathcal{O}(\omega/T)\right) with some constant cc [96], and from (61) it follows that the phonon frequency (pole of Ga​(ω)G_{a}(\omega)) is shifted downwards. Importantly, this provides an experimentally accessible signature of the DSL via monopole-phonon couplings, in particular also in parameter regimes where the spin liquid is expected to be stable. The softening of the phonon will exhibit a power-law scaling with temperature with a (universal) exponent that depends on the monopole operator dimension as a characteristic signature of the Dirac spin liquid.

We can find an explicit solution to the equation (61) by considering ω→0\omega\to 0 and T>0T>0. In this case, above scaling form for χa′\chi_{a}^{\prime} becomes exact, yielding 0=ω02−g2​|𝒌a|2​ρ−1​χa′​(0,T)0=\omega_{0}^{2}-g^{2}|{\bm{k}}_{a}|^{2}\rho^{-1}\chi^{\prime}_{a}(0,T). This is solved when 1∼g2​|𝒌a|2​κ−1​T−(3−2​ΔΦ)1\sim g^{2}|{\bm{k}}_{a}|^{2}\kappa^{-1}T^{-(3-2\Delta_{\Phi})}, which precisely recovers the critical scaling of the spin-Peierls temperature TSPT_{\mathrm{SP}} as a function of gg in Eq. (32). At this critical temperature, the softened phonon hits zero energy and condenses, giving rise to a finite static lattice distortion as discussed in Sec. V.

Conversely, we can analyze the zero-temperature T→0T\to 0 limit in (61) working perturbatively: If the second term on the right-hand side of (61) is much smaller than first term, one can perturbatively solve the implicit equation by iteratively substituting (the square-root of) the left-hand side for ω\omega on the right-hand side, generating an order-by-order expansion. To leading order, we thus obtain

ω2≈ω02−g2​|𝒌a|2​ρ−1​χa′​(ω0,0)+….\omega^{2}\approx\omega_{0}^{2}-g^{2}|{\bm{k}}_{a}|^{2}\rho^{-1}\chi_{a}^{\prime}(\omega_{0},0)+\dots. (62)

Using χa′​(ω,0)∼ω−(3−2​ΔΦ)\chi_{a}^{\prime}(\omega,0)\sim\omega^{-(3-2\Delta_{\Phi})}, again fixed by scaling [41, 96], one obtains that the phonon dispersion is renormalized down to zero energy ω=0\omega=0 when 1∼g2​|𝒌a|2​κ−1​ω0−(3−2​ΔΦ)1\sim g^{2}|{\bm{k}}_{a}|^{2}\kappa^{-1}\omega_{0}^{-(3-2\Delta_{\Phi})}, which coincides with the parameter regime where the perturbative treatment of (61) breaks down, and yields the scaling law (59) for the critical spin-Peierls coupling at finite frequency and zero-temperature.

While above analysis was focussed on the dynamics of the phonon modes at the relevant wavevectors 𝒌a{\bm{k}}_{a}, one can extend the interacting phonon propagator Ga​(ω)=G⁡(ω,𝒌a)G_{a}(\omega)=G(\omega,{\bm{k}}_{a}) in Eq. (60) to momenta 𝒌a+δ​𝒒{\bm{k}}_{a}+\delta{\bm{q}} around 𝒌a{\bm{k}}_{a} (with |δ​𝒒|≪|δ​𝒌a||\delta{\bm{q}}|\ll|\delta{\bm{k}}_{a}|) given a microscopic model for the bare phonon dispersion ω0​(𝒒)\omega_{0}({\bm{q}}), as e.g. in (23). With the zero-temperature form of the monopole susceptibility χ⁡(ω,𝒌a+δ​𝒒)=[c2​|δ​𝒒|2−ω2]−(3/2−ΔΦ)\chi(\omega,{\bm{k}}_{a}+\delta{\bm{q}})=[c^{2}|\delta{\bm{q}}|^{2}-\omega^{2}]^{-(3/2-\Delta_{\Phi})}, the phonon spectral function (at second order perturbation theory) can be calculated as shown in Appendix E. Turning to finite temperatures, we note that the monopole susceptibility can be written in terms of some unknown scaling function, but in contrast to (1+1)-dimensional quantum critical theories, there does not exist a conformal mapping which would allow us to extract the dynamical response at finite temperatures. Gaining an in-depth understanding of finite-temperature dynamical correlations of the DSL is a highly interesting task for future theoretical and computational studies [96, 97].

VIII Conclusion & Outlook

VIII.1 Summary

We have studied the effective theory of the U(1) Dirac spin liquid in the presence of lattice distortions. The effective low-energy description of spinons coupled to a dynamical gauge field is QED3\text{QED}_{3} with Nf=4N_{f}=4 fermions which is believed to flow to a strongly coupled conformal fixed point in the continuum. The compactness of the dynamical gauge field allows for monopoles as instanton tunneling events which insert a 2​π2\pi flux of the emergent gauge field. While on the triangular lattice these operators are relevant, they carry non-trivial quantum numbers under the microscopic UV lattice symmetry, and the isolated DSL is expected to be stable.

Crucially, we have shown that there exists a symmetry-allowed coupling between lattice distortions at finite wavevectors 𝑲a/2{\bm{K}}_{a}/2 (where 𝑲1,2,3{\bm{K}}_{1,2,3} are the corners of the hexagonal Brillouin zone) to spin-singlet, valley-triplet monopoles that act as order parameters for VBS ordering. Considering static distortion fields, this coupling induces an instability of the DSL which can be understood as a direct analog of the spin-Peierls instability of the 1+1-dimensional Luttinger liquid, similarly driven by the proliferation of instanton events.

We have analyzed the coupling of monopoles to static lattice distortions first within conformal perturbation theory with a finite-temperature regularization, leading to a critical temperature Tc∼(gc2/K)1/(3−2​ΔΦ)T_{c}\sim(g^{2}_{c}/K)^{1/(3-2\Delta_{\Phi})} below which the DSL becomes unstable. In a complementary approach, we have employed a scaling ansatz to find that the energy of static lattice distortions uu lower the ground-state energy of the DSL Δ​E∼−uχ\Delta E\sim-u^{\chi} with χ<2\chi<2, which generally outcompetes the harmonic elastic energy Eelast∼u2E_{\mathrm{elast}}\sim u^{2}, therefore favoring an equilibrium lattice distortion.

In both approaches, we found that the space of possible lattice distortion patterns and spontaneous VBS orderings exhibits accidental (continous) symmetries as artifacts of the low-energy theory. Symmetry-allowed three-monopole operators may be dangerously irrelevant and can lift these accidental degeneracies, and we predict a resulting VBS order with a 12-site unit cell that preserves a C3C_{3} symmetry of the lattice.

We have provided supporting evidence for our theoretical predictions via DMRG calculations for the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} model on the triangular lattice. We manually distorted the lattice and modified its couplings depending on modified bond lengths from our predicted distortion and measure the ground state energy as a function of system size. We found the in general quadratic energy to be strongest for 12-site pattern. Despite the difficulty of simulating strongly-frustrated triangular lattice Heisenberg models, we were able to observe signatures of ground state VBS order in agreement to the field-theoretical predictions. Furthermore, we use finite-size scaling to deduce from within our microscopic model (UV scales) that distortions at 𝑲/2{\bm{K}}/2 are strongly relevant perturbations to the DSL, as predicted by the low-energy IR field theory.

In addition to the conclusions drawn above, we highlight that this result provides compelling additional evidence of a gapless U(1) DSL ground state of the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} triangular lattice Heisenberg model and highlight the predictive power of the low-energy QED3 theory for numerical simulations. Despite computational limitations that introduce e.g., finite-size gaps, a detailed system-size scaling study can capture behavior characteristic of an underlying conformal fixed point. These methods have strong predictive power which is indispensable when looking to connect theory with experimental results.

Finally, we have considered the case of dynamic (non-dispersive) phonons, with some frequency ω0>0\omega_{0}>0. At finite frequencies, these degrees of freedom can be integrated out and yield an effective action containing retarded monopole-monopole interactions which have not been analyzed previously. We showed that the spin-Peierls instability now occurs at finite couplings gc>0g_{c}>0, while in the stable regime the phonon spectrum is strongly renormalized. We summarize our results in the ‘scaling phase diagram’ shown in Fig. 6, where we schematically indicate the parameter regime where an instability of the DSL is expected to occur.

VIII.2 Application to other systems

VIII.2.1 Kagome lattice

Our general framework and formalism can be straightforwardly applied to the U⁡(1)\mathrm{U(1)} DSL state on the Kagome lattice [25, 38]. On the Kagome lattice, the UV symmetry quantum numbers of the monopoles are different than those on the triangular lattice. In particular, the VBS monopoles carry lattice momenta 𝑴a{\bm{M}}_{a}, corresponding to the Brillouin zone edge centers. Further, under C6C_{6} rotations, they pick up an additional phase: saΦa→sa+1e−2πi/3Φa+1s_{a}\Phi_{a}\rightarrow s_{a+1}\mathrm{e}^{-2\pi\mathrm{i}/3}\Phi_{a+1}, and under reflection RR the monopoles transform as Table. 1 but with an additional Hermitian conjugation [38]. The construction of the monopole-lattice coupling is complicated by the fact that the non-Bravais Kagome lattice has three sites per unit cells such that there are 6 (3 longitudinal + 3 transverse) distortion modes for a given lattice momentum.

Based on the previous analysis, we can focus on the longitudinal modes on the sublattice X=A,B,CX=A,B,C (an intra-unit cell index) and momenta 𝑴a{\bm{M}}_{a} which we label as uX​(𝑴a)u_{X}({\bm{M}}_{a}). Under the symmetry operations, the different (real) Fourier components with wavevectors 𝑴a{\bm{M}}_{a} are mapped onto each other (corresponding to changing monopole flavors). Simultaneouly, the intra-unit cell coordinates X=A,B,CX=A,B,C are appropriately mapped into each other (this intra-unitcell contribution is similar to the ‘pseudo-angular momentum’ contribution of chiral phonons under C6C_{6} as studied in Ref. [98]). Hence, the XX components can be decomposed with respect to the irreducible representations (irreps) of C3​v≃𝒮3C_{3v}\simeq\mathcal{S}_{3} (the permutation group of three elements), which possesses three (complex) one-dimensional irreps which can be labeled by their C3C_{3} eigenvalues. Choosing the appropriate irrep, hah_{a}, that cancels out the additional phase factors of the monopoles under C6C_{6} rotations, allows us to write the couplings

Sg[h→]∼g(e2​π​i/3h1Φ1+h2Φ2−e−2πi/3h3Φ3+h.c.).S_{g}[\vec{h}]\sim g\left(\mathrm{e}^{2\pi\mathrm{i}/3}h_{1}\Phi_{1}+h_{2}\Phi_{2}-\mathrm{e}^{-2\pi\mathrm{i}/3}h_{3}\Phi_{3}+\mathrm{h.c.}\right). (63)

Having obtained the coupling, the results from Sec. V carry over straightforwardly; the coupling precipitates an instability towards VBS ordering and lattice distortion. Transforming back to the sublattice basis X=A,B,CX=A,B,C, the longitudinal phonon which couples to the monopoles is obtained by relative 2​π/32\pi/3 phases uX​(𝑴a)=e2​π​i​X/3​hau_{X}({\bm{M}}_{a})=\mathrm{e}^{2\pi\mathrm{i}\,X/3}h_{a}, allowing us to predict the lattice distortion as in Fig. 7. Identifying symmetry-equivalent expressions of the monopole operators in terms of microscopic spin bilinears as in (14), we can additionally characterize the resulting ordered state on a microscopic level as the ‘pinwheel’ VBS order [99, 100].

VIII.2.2 Square and honeycomb lattice

On the square and honeycomb lattice, the U⁡(1)\mathrm{U(1)} DSL is intrinsically unstable [38] due to the presence of relevant monopole operators that are singlets under all UV symmetries 22 2 Technically, this statement refers to the well-established staggered-flux and 00-flux states on the square and honeycomb lattices that were studied in Ref. [38]. As shown in Ref. [133], there may exist stable DSL states on square and honeycomb lattice, though no parton constructions are known.. Furthermore, while stable ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquids exist on these lattices, they will not exhibit spin-Peierls instabilities due to the gapped nature of gauge excitations. This applies equally to the gapless phase of the Kitaev honeycomb model, which is known to not generically exhibit a spontaneous Kekulé distortion at weak coupling [60, 61].

VIII.2.3 Spin-orbital models: extending to general NfN_{f}

Going beyond S=1/2S=1/2, some spin-orbital models with intrinsic SU⁡(4)\mathrm{SU(4)} symmetry have been found to exhibit disordered ground states with algebraically decaying correlations [102, 103]. Such spin-orbital liquids could be described by QED3\text{QED}_{3} with Nf=8N_{f}=8 fermion flavors [104]. Within the large-NfN_{f} approximation, the monopole has dimension ΔΦ=0.2651​Nf−0.0381+𝒪⁡(1/Nf)\Delta_{\Phi}=0.2651N_{f}-0.0381+\mathcal{O}(1/N_{f}) [105, 74]. While this implies a lattice-monopole coupling is relevant for all Nf<12N_{f}<12, we find it only precipitates an instability for Nf<6N_{f}<6. To see this, note that both the perturbative approach in Eq. (30) as well as the scaling ansatz [see Eq. (34)] place a stronger constraint ΔΦ<3/2\Delta_{\Phi}<3/2 for the system to undergo the spin-Peierls instability due to the harmonic energy cost of lattice distortions. Hence we do not expect a weak-coupling spin-Peierls instability in the U⁡(1)\mathrm{U(1)} Dirac spin-orbital liquid, despite the presence of relevant monopole operators.

VIII.2.4 Generalization to dd dimensions

Our results can be understood as 2+1-dim. extension of the spin-Peierls instability of interacting spin-half chains in 1+1 dimensions. We found an instability when lattice distortions couple to an operator with scaling dimension ΔΦ<d/2\Delta_{\Phi}<d/2, which is in accordance with the collapse of quantum criticality [106, 107] when ν⁡(D+z)−2<0\nu(D+z)-2<0 in D=d−1D=d-1 spatial dimensions with dynamical exponent z=1z=1 and correlation length exponent ν−1=d−ΔΦ\nu^{-1}=d-\Delta_{\Phi} 33 3 Any linear coupling to monopoles, 𝒮∼g​h​Φ+h.c.\mathcal{S}\sim gh\,\Phi+\mathrm{h.c.}, introduces a length scale to the otherwise scale-invariant theory, which we can identify as a correlation length ξ\xi. By powercounting, we have |gh|∼ξ−(3−ΔΦ)⇔ξ∼|gh|−1/(3−ΔΦ)|gh|\sim\xi^{-(3-\Delta_{\Phi})}\Leftrightarrow\xi\sim|gh|^{-1/(3-\Delta_{\Phi})} from which we can read off the correlation length exponent ν\nu.. We emphasize that this result is more restrictive than the mere relevance of the monopole operator, ΔΦ<d\Delta_{\Phi}<d.

To illustrate this point, we can revisit the (d=2+1)(d=2+1)-dim. CFT of free Dirac fermions, for concreteness as a low-energy theory of e.g., graphene or the honeycomb lattice Kitaev model. While a Kekulé distortion uu couples via g​u​ψ​ψ¯gu\,\psi\overline{\psi} to the relevant fermion mass operator M=ψ¯​ψM=\bar{\psi}\psi with ΔM=2\Delta_{M}=2, the system is stable since ΔM>3/2\Delta_{M}>3/2. This stable free-fermion CFT is also obtained from QED3\text{QED}_{3} in the limit Nf→∞N_{f}\rightarrow\infty; we therefore stress that the spin-Peierls instability of the DSL crucially depends on strong gauge fluctuations in QED3 at finite Nf=4N_{f}=4. This matches the intuition from interacting Luttinger liquids, where fermion interactions enhance the spin-Peierels instability compared to the free-fermion (equiv. to the spin-1/2 XY chain) due to instantons becoming more relevant.

VIII.3 Outlook

Our results for the DSL highlight that the coupling of quantum-critical states to other degrees of freedom can dramatically affect their stability. In a similar vein, it will be interesting to study the impact of coupling other critical deconfined states to lattice degrees of freedom, such as deconfined quantum critical points [82, 109, 110] or non-Lagrangian QSL phases [111]. Such couplings may not only generate instabilities, but can also provide a route to resolve critical correlations via, e.g., anomalies in phonon spectra [110].

Turning towards experiments, we note that recently several triangular-lattice candidate materials have been identified, such as NaYbO2 [112, 113] and YbZn2GaO5 [114], which exhibit broad inelastic neutron-scattering spectra and, importantly, a T2T^{2}-scaling of the magnetic specific heat at low temperatures, suggestive of Dirac-type gapless excitations.

An open question on the road to confirmation of the realization in materials pertains to the fate of such state against quenched disorder [115, 116], lattice defects, and additional degrees of freedom, such as interlayer coupling or indeed also phonons as studied here. These are inevitably present in solid-state systems and a detailed understanding of their impact on QSLs will help in determining whether candidate materials display signatures of more trivial origin.

The VBS-ordered phase that is generated via the spin-Peierls instability is accompanied by a finite lattice distortion, which we expect to be measurable, e.g. by sensitive inelastic X-ray scattering experiments (as in spin-chain compounds [117]). The spin-Peierls mechanism could be disentangled from intrinsic structural distortions by studying the magnetic-field-dependence of critical temperatures [118]. It will be interesting to explore to what extent a spin-Peierls mechanism might be consistent with a recent report of a gapped ground state with finite structural distortion in an organic salt triangular lattice spin-liquid candidate material [119].

Turning to the kagome lattice, pinwheel VBS ground states have been measured on the deformed kagome-lattice antiferromagnetic Heisenberg compound Rb2Cu3SnF12 [120, 100]. This material exhibits a lattice distortion which is compatible with the predicted spin-Peierls pattern of the DSL on the Kagome lattice. Although the presence of a lattice distortion at high temperature points towards a non-magnetic origin, it would be interesting to explore whether there are universal arguments that favor such pinwheel distortion patterns, possibly by considering incoherent high-temperature dynamics of the U⁡(1)\mathrm{U(1)} DSL. We note that although previous numerical studies of the kagome-lattice Heisenberg model with a simpler 12-site distortion pattern have suggested an unusually small nonzero critical coupling αc>0\alpha_{c}>0 [121, 122], our zero-temperature results conclude that the pinwheel VBS is precipitated for any finite lattice-coupling αc=0\alpha_{c}=0 if the U(1) DSL is acting as an organizing or parent state for this material.

In real materials, phonons at finite momenta have non-zero frequency, and we have identified a power-law parameter regime where the spin-liquid is expected to be stable down to lowest temperatures. Our study therefore places constraints on the realization and observability of the U⁡(1)\mathrm{U(1)} Dirac spin liquid in materials. Within stable DSL phase, a monopole-phonon coupling is responsible for a Kohn-type anomaly visible in the phonon spectrum. Therefore, phonon spectra may provide (indirect) insights into the critical correlations of a Dirac spin liquid, similar to elastic signatures of quantum critical points [123, 124, 107].

It is in the purview of future numerical work to evaluate the stable parameter regime of the DSL and predict the magnitude of potential experimental signatures quantitatively, starting from realistic microscopic spin models and experimentally applicable phonon spectra. The treatment of quantum phonons coupled to a QSL is especially computationally challenging but would allow for a more realistic modeling of candidate materials given exchange parameters and bare phonon frequency.

Our work also implies that the coupling to lattice degrees of freedom may provide a fruitful route to distinguish between different types of gapless spin liquids: Spin-singlet monopoles are reflected in observables such as phonon spectra (via the Kohn-like softening), or potentially Raman spectra (see also the recent proposals of Ref. [77]). In this context, we mention that the singular response of the DSL to externally induced lattice displacements, in particular via strain, may provide a key signature for the experimental characterization of possible DSL phases.

The spin-Peierls instability of the Luttinger liquid in one-dimensional spin chains has been one of the paradigmatic examples of strong quantum fluctuations in low-dimensional quantum many-body systems. The U⁡(1)\mathrm{U(1)} DSL, described by a strongly interacting field theory, constitutes a similarly remarkable new phase of matter in two dimensions which we have shown also exhibits a spin-Peierls instability. We hope that a better understanding of the stability of QSLs with respect to coupling to phonons or lattice disorder will help for the eventual discovery of these enigmatic quantum liquids in real materials.

Appendix A Luttinger liquid and XXZ model

The XXZ model reads

HXXZ=∑iJx​y​(Six​Si+1x+Siy​Si+1y)+Jz​Siz​Si+1z,H_{\mathrm{XXZ}}=\sum_{i}J_{xy}(S^{x}_{i}S^{x}_{i+1}+S^{y}_{i}S^{y}_{i+1})+J_{z}S^{z}_{i}S^{z}_{i+1}, (64)

where tuning Δ=Jz/Jx​y\Delta=J_{z}/J_{xy} tunes between the XY (Δ=0\Delta=0) and AFM Heisenberg model (Δ=1\Delta=1) [17]. The bozonisation procedure maps this onto a continuum field theory

H⁡[ϕ⁡(x)]=12​π​∫d2x⁡[K​(∂tϕ)2+1K​(∂xϕ)2]+V4∫d2xcos⁡(4​ϕ),H[\phi(x)]=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int\differential[2]{x}\left[K(\partial_{t}\phi)^{2}+\frac{1}{K}(\partial_{x}\phi)^{2}\right]\\ +V_{4}\int\differential[2]{x}\cos(4\phi), (65)

The kinetic term describes a free boson, where the Luttinger parameter KK characterizes the quasi-long range order and is also fixed by the microscopic bosonization mapping. In the XY model, it takes the value K=12K=\frac{1}{2}, and in the isotropic Heisenberg model it has the value 22.

The term V4V_{4} is an interaction strength of the instanton cos⁡(4​ϕ)\cos(4\phi). An instanton tunnels between distinct ground states, introducing a winding in the periodic variable ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x). The symmetries of the original lattice constrain the possible interactions that can appear in the effective bosonized description. Most relevant for our study, the discrete translational symmetry of the chain under Si→Si+1S_{i}\to S_{i+1} manifests as a constraint that the effective theory is invariant under ϕ→ϕ+π/2\phi\to\phi+\pi/2. Therefore all interactions must be of the form of derivatives or periodic functions Vn​cos⁡(n​ϕ)V_{n}\cos(n\phi) with n≥4n\geq 4. Similarly, inversion symmetry requires the function be symmetric under ϕ⁡(x)→−ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x)\to-\phi(x), which forbids terms of the form Wn​sin⁡(n​ϕ)W_{n}\sin(n\phi).

Given in terms of the microscopic spin Hamiltonian, the interaction is V~4=Jz/2\tilde{V}_{4}=J^{z}/2 at lattice length scales ∼𝖺\sim\mathsf{a}. The XY model with Jz=0J^{z}=0 is therefore effectively described by a free massless boson at the UV scale. To describe long-wavelength behavior, one must understand how couplings flow; to this end, we write Vn​(ζ)=ζ2−Δn​V~nV_{n}(\zeta)=\zeta^{2-\Delta_{n}}\tilde{V}_{n} at length scales ζ​𝖺\zeta\mathsf{a}. Expanding around the Gaussian fixed point, it can be shown that interactions of the form cos⁡(n​ϕ)\cos(n\phi) have a scaling dimension of Δn=n2​K/4\Delta_{n}=n^{2}\,K/4. If an operator is relevant, then Δn<2\Delta_{n}<2 and the coupling grows in the IR ζ→∞\zeta\to\infty. Such an operator induces a mass scale in the spectrum M⁡(ζ)=Vn​(ζ)χn/2=ζ​V~nχn/2M(\zeta)=V_{n}(\zeta)^{\chi_{n}/2}=\zeta\,\tilde{V}_{n}^{\chi_{n}/2} with χn=2/(2−Δn)\chi_{n}=2/(2-\Delta_{n}).

The instanton cos⁡(4​ϕ)\cos(4\phi) has dimension Δ4=4​K\Delta_{4}=4K, which for the Heisenberg model K=1/2K=1/2 is marginally irrelevant [17]. This means the system has a stable spin-liquid-like ground state with gapless excitations in the IR. The stability of this phase is protected by the lattice symmetries, as a more relevant instanton cos⁡(2​ϕ)\cos(2\phi) would be relevant at this Heisenberg point, but is forbidden on symmetry grounds. For any lower K<1/2K<1/2 (from OPENJz>Jx​y)J_{z}>J_{xy}), the interaction V4V_{4} becomes relevant and the spectrum becomes gapped. In terms of the fermions, there is a Mott transition; in terms of the spins, the model enters the Ising universality class.

Appendix B Conformal field theory & conformal data

In the following, we will refrain from working with the explicit formulation of the field theory ℒQED3\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}} in terms of strongly interacting ψ,aμ\psi,a_{\mu} and having to account for monopoles as non-trivial background configurations. Instead, we exploit the description of the IR fixed point as a conformal field theory (CFT) in 2+1 dimensions, which is characterized by its conformal data, consisting of (1) a spectrum of scaling operators and (2) the operator product expansion.

B.1 Scaling operators

For N=4N=4-flavor QED3\text{QED}_{3}, the lowest-lying operators are given by the six charge-1 monopole operators. The gauge-invariant combination of monopole operators and two Dirac zero modes fα†f_{\alpha}^{\dagger} reads [38]

Φα​β†∼fα†​fβ†​ℳ2​π†,\Phi^{\dagger}_{\alpha\beta}\sim f_{\alpha}^{\dagger}f_{\beta}^{\dagger}\mathcal{M}_{2\pi}^{\dagger}, (66)

where α,β\alpha,\beta are SU⁡(4)\mathrm{SU(4)}-indices. As written here, Φα​β†\Phi_{\alpha\beta}^{\dagger} transforms in the antisymmetric rank-2 representation 𝟔\mathbf{6} of SU⁡(4)\mathrm{SU(4)}. It is convenient to use the isomorphism SO⁡(6)=SU⁡(4)/ℤ2\mathrm{SO}(6)=\mathrm{SU(4)}/\mathbb{Z}_{2}, such that we can take Φa†\Phi^{\dagger}_{a} with a=1,…,6a=1,\dots,6 to transform as a six-dimensional vector. A recent CFT bootstrap study [37] estimates the scaling dimension ΔΦ∈(1.02,1.04)\Delta_{\Phi}\in(1.02,1.04), very similar to the large-NN (subleading order) result ΔΦ≈1.02\Delta_{\Phi}\approx 1.02 [36]. Other numerical works give similar estimates for ΔΦ\Delta_{\Phi} [35, 126].

The next lowest-lying operators are the adjoint fermion masses

Mα​β=ψ¯​σα​τβ​ψM^{\alpha\beta}=\overline{\psi}\sigma^{\alpha}\tau^{\beta}\psi (67)

with α,β=0,1,2,3\alpha,\beta=0,1,2,3 and σ\sigma/τ\tau act on spin/valley indices of the fermions. The masses Mα​βM^{\alpha\beta} transform in a sixteen-dimensional reducible representation of SU⁡(4)\mathrm{SU(4)}, which splits into the singlet and adjoint irreducible representations 𝟏𝟔=𝟏⊕𝟏𝟓\mathbf{16}=\mathbf{1}\oplus\mathbf{15}.

The scaling dimension of the adjoint mass term Mμ​νM^{\mu\nu} (with μ=ν=0\mu=\nu=0 excluded) is strongly relevant, with ΔM=1.46\Delta_{M}=1.46 in the large-NfN_{f} expansion [36] and ΔM∈(1.33,1.66)\Delta_{M}\in(1.33,1.66) according to a recent bootstrap study [37]. Due to their non-trivial representations under lattice transformations, these perturbations cannot trivially be added to the action. On the triangular lattice the symmetry-allowed four-fermion interaction is believed to be irrelevant [127].

The singlet M00M_{00} corresponds to a chiral mass term and can be tuned to produce a chiral spin liquid state. In large-NfN_{f}, this term is irrelevant Δ0=3.08\Delta_{0}=3.08, and thus it is believed that spontaneous chiral symmetry breaking does not occur [71, 72, 73].

B.2 Operator product expansion

The operator product expansion (OPE) states how operators approaching each other are expanded in the basis of primaries as

limx→y𝒪i​(x)​𝒪j​(y)=limx→y∑kCi​jk|x−y|Δi+Δj−Δk​𝒪k​(y),\lim_{x\to y}\mathcal{O}_{i}(x)\mathcal{O}_{j}(y)=\lim_{x\to y}\sum_{k}\frac{C_{ij}^{k}}{|x-y|^{\Delta_{i}+\Delta_{j}-\Delta_{k}}}\mathcal{O}_{k}(y), (68)

where the Ci​jkC_{ij}^{k} are the OPE coefficients. If the CFT is endowed with some global symmetry group 𝒢\mathcal{G}, each term on the RHS of (68) will transform in some irreducible representation of 𝒢×𝒢\mathcal{G}\times\mathcal{G}. We stress that Eq. (68) corresponds to the asymptotic formulation of the OPE, but in general, OPEs can be shown to be convergent series if all primaries and their descendants are included. The full asymptotic form of the operators can be written in terms of the two real OPE coefficents CΦ​ΦMC_{\Phi\Phi}^{M} and CM​ΦΦC_{M\Phi}^{\Phi} in the following way:

Φa†​(x)​Φb​(y)∼δa​b|x−y|2​ΔΦ+i​CΦ​ΦM|x−y|2​ΔΦ−ΔM​ℱμ​νa​b​Mμ​ν​(y)+…\displaystyle\Phi_{a}^{\dagger}(x)\Phi_{b}(y)\sim\frac{\delta_{ab}}{|x-y|^{2\Delta_{\Phi}}}+\frac{\mathrm{i}C_{\Phi\Phi}^{M}}{|x-y|^{2\Delta_{\Phi}-\Delta_{M}}}\mathcal{F}^{ab}_{\mu\nu}M^{\mu\nu}(y)+\dots (69a)
Φa​(x)​Mμ​ν​(y)∼i​CΦ​MΦ|x−y|ΔM​ℱ¯a​bμ​ν​Φb​(y)+…,\displaystyle\Phi_{a}(x)M^{\mu\nu}(y)\sim\frac{\mathrm{i}C_{\Phi M}^{\Phi}}{|x-y|^{\Delta_{M}}}\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{ab}^{\mu\nu}\Phi_{b}(y)+\dots, (69b)

where the tensor ℱμ​νa​b\mathcal{F}^{ab}_{\mu\nu} maps elements of the adjoint-SU⁡(4)\mathrm{SU(4)} representation to rank-2 antisymmetric representations of SO⁡(6)\mathrm{SO}(6) and ℱ¯a​bμ​ν\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{ab}^{\mu\nu} its inverse. Implicit sums over (μ,ν)(\mu,\nu) are taken to exclude the (0,0)(0,0) element. The nonzero components are ℱ0​ia​b=ϵa​b​i\mathcal{F}_{0i}^{ab}=\epsilon^{abi} for a,b≤3a,b\leq 3; ℱ0​ia​b=ϵa−3,b−3,i\mathcal{F}_{0i}^{ab}=\epsilon^{a-3,b-3,i} for a,b>3a,b>3; and ℱi​ja​b=δja​δi+3b−δi+3a​δjb\mathcal{F}_{ij}^{ab}=\delta_{j}^{a}\delta^{b}_{i+3}-\delta_{i+3}^{a}\delta^{b}_{j}, as defined in Ref. [79]. Here, the components i,j=1,2,3i,j=1,2,3. We can also write the components of its inverse ℱ¯a​bμ​ν=ℱμ​νa​b/2\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{ab}^{\mu\nu}=\mathcal{F}^{ab}_{\mu\nu}/2.

Appendix C Fermion masses coupled to the lattice

C.1 Effective action including fermion mass couplings

In the main text, we constructed an effective action of VBS monopoles coupled to lattice distortions by considering the leading contributions from a redefinition of the lattice 𝑹i→𝑹i+𝒖i{\bm{R}}_{i}\to{\bm{R}}_{i}+{\bm{u}}_{i}.

In this section we will approach the task of constructing an effective theory of QED3\text{QED}_{3} coupled to a lattice distortion using a ‘top-down’, symmetry-based approach. This path allows us to categorize couplings to all possible operators in the theory which could contribute to a ground state instability. This approach validates the previous method by showing that the monopole indeed causes the leading instability and that the subleading operators couple to the same momentum modes of the lattice distortion.

We now write down a general set of couplings to the leading relevant operators in QED3\text{QED}_{3}: the monopoles Φa\Phi_{a} (a=1​…​6a=1\dots 6) and adjoint fermion masses Mμ​νM_{\mu\nu} [μ,ν=0​…​3\mu,\nu=0\dots 3, (μ,ν)≠(0,0)](\mu,\nu)\neq(0,0)]. The general form of this action is

S∼∫d3x[∑a=16(φa∗Φa(x)+h.c.)+∑μ,νmμ​νMμ​ν(x)].S\sim\int\differential[3]{x}\left[\sum_{a=1}^{6}\left(\varphi_{a}^{*}\Phi_{a}(x)+\mathrm{h.c.}\right)+\sum_{\mu,\nu}m_{\mu\nu}M^{\mu\nu}(x)\right]. (70)

The monopoles transform under the UV symmetries as listed in Table 1, and the masses as listed in Table 2. We will preserve the lattice symmetries by constructing an appropriate object hah_{a} that transforms in the same representation as Φa\Phi_{a} of the IR emergent symmetry group SU⁡(4)\mathrm{SU(4)}. Because the UV lattice symmetries embed in this emergent group, constructing an invariant SU⁡(4)\mathrm{SU(4)}-scalar is equivalent to writing an function that is invariant under lattice symmetries.

For our physical system of interest, the question becomes whether it is possible to construct a vector hah_{a} that transforms as the monopole under physical symmetries in Table 1 out of the physical lattice-distortion vector field 𝒖⁡(𝒙){\bm{u}}({\bm{x}}). This object will naturally transform as a vector under the SO​(3)valley\mathrm{SO(3)}_{\mathrm{valley}} subgroup of the full SO⁡(6)\mathrm{SO}(6), and not transform under SO​(3)spin\mathrm{SO(3)}_{\mathrm{spin}}.

To classify all perturbations that could be symmetry-allowed in the presence of a deformation vector 𝒖𝒒{\bm{u}}_{{\bm{q}}}, we must restrict our search by using the following criteria: (1) consider distortions which are periodic with wavevector 𝒒{\bm{q}} that is equal to that of the field theory operator and (2) are fully invariant under the discrete subgroups C6C_{6}, 𝒯\mathcal{T}. These two requirements will be equivalent to restricting to coupling field theory operators to fields which are vectors under SO​(3)valley\mathrm{SO(3)}_{\mathrm{valley}} and trivial under SO​(3)valley\mathrm{SO(3)}_{\mathrm{valley}}. Finally, by way of the correspondence between vector and adjoint representations, one can write down an object bilinear in the lattice deformation field which can couple to field theory objects in the SO​(3)valley\mathrm{SO(3)}_{\mathrm{valley}}-adjoint representation.

We satisfy the above constraints by defining field hah_{a} as

ha=i​sa​(𝒌a⋅𝒖𝒌a),h_{a}=\mathrm{i}s_{a}({\bm{k}}_{a}\cdot{\bm{u}}_{{\bm{k}}_{a}}), (71)

where we have chosen 𝒌a{\bm{k}}_{a} as a basis of three vectors separated by 2​π/32\pi/3 angles. It satisfies translational invariance since it has the same momentum eigenvalue as the monopole, and also transforms as a vector under SO​(3)valley\mathrm{SO(3)}_{\mathrm{valley}}. Under IR symmetries it transforms as the VBS monopole, as listed in Table 1. We see it is possible to preserve the full lattice symmetry group by coupling this field to the monopoles and masses as follows:

φa∗=gha∗,m0​a=imℱb​c0​ahb∗hc,a=1,2,3,\varphi_{a}^{*}=g\,h_{a}^{*},\quad m_{0a}=\mathrm{i}m\,\mathcal{F}^{bc}_{0a}h_{b}^{*}h_{c},\quad a=1,2,3, (72)

where the non-zero components give m0​a=i​m​ϵa​b​c​hb∗​hcm_{0a}=\mathrm{i}m\,\epsilon^{abc}h_{b}^{*}h_{c}.

We can exclude any direct linear coupling of lattice distortions to spin-triplet monopoles Φa\Phi_{a}, a=4,5,6a=4,5,6. In terms of the discrete symmetries this follows since under the C6C_{6} transformation Φa→−Φa†\Phi_{a}\to-\Phi_{a}^{\dagger}. This is incompatible with any coupling to a vector 𝒖a{\bm{u}}_{a}, which necessarily rotates under such an operation 𝒖a→−𝒖a+1∗{\bm{u}}_{a}\to-{\bm{u}}^{*}_{a+1}.

We could instead attempt to couple distortions hah_{a} directly to the valley-triplet fermion masses Mi​aM_{ia}, and then generate monopole couplings by using the inverse mapping between 2-dimensional and adjoint representations. However these masses also transform in the index ii as a spin-vector, which could provide a hindrance to writing an invariant action. Inspecting the behavior under lattice symmetries (Table 2), we find the coupling satisfies translational invariance (1) when coupling to the (real) modes at the 𝑴1,2,3{\bm{M}}_{1,2,3}-points on the Brillouin zone edges 𝒖~a=𝒖𝑴a\tilde{{\bm{u}}}_{a}={{\bm{u}}}_{{\bm{M}}_{a}}. We are therefore motivated to write the couplings m~i,g~i\tilde{m}_{i},\tilde{g}_{i} for i=1,2,3i=1,2,3,

mi​a=m~ih~a,φa=−ig~iℱb​ci​ah~bh~c,a=1,2,3,m_{ia}=\tilde{m}_{i}\tilde{h}_{a},\quad\varphi_{a}=-\mathrm{i}\tilde{g}_{i}\,{\mathcal{F}}_{bc}^{ia}\tilde{h}^{b}\tilde{h}^{c},\quad a=1,2,3, (73)

with non-zero components giving φ~a+3=−i​g~b​h~a​h~b\tilde{\varphi}_{a+3}=-\mathrm{i}\tilde{g}_{b}\tilde{h}_{a}\tilde{h}_{b}. However there is no choice of h~a\tilde{h}_{a} which leaves mi​a​Mi​am_{ia}M^{ia} invariant under both discrete lattice symmetries (2). For this reason, we must exclude a direct coupling between fermion masses and the 𝑴{\bm{M}} points from the effective action.

We are now able to write the full symmetry-allowed action at lowest order in relevant operators as a sum of VBS monopole and mass terms,

SI[ha]=∫d3x[g(ha∗Φa(x)+h.c.)+imϵa​b​chb∗hcM0​a(x)],S_{I}[h_{a}]=\int\differential[3]{x}\left[g\left(h_{a}^{*}\,\Phi_{a}(x)+\mathrm{h.c.}\right)+\mathrm{i}m\,\epsilon^{abc}h^{*}_{b}h_{c}\,M_{0a}(x)\right], (74)

both of which are coupled to lattice distortions via ha=i​sa​(𝒌a⋅𝒖𝒌a)h_{a}=\mathrm{i}s_{a}({\bm{k}}_{a}\cdot{\bm{u}}_{{\bm{k}}_{a}}). There is furthermore a set of compound operators which may be added as deformations to the theory. One example is the triple-monopole term Φ1​Φ2​Φ3\Phi_{1}\Phi_{2}\Phi_{3}; allowed even on the undistorted lattice, this term is irrelevant at the conformal IR fixed point. One can equally construct double-monopole terms coupled to a commensurate lattice distortion (or appropriate combination thereof). At this point we will ignore such compound operators which have a scaling dimension Δ>3/2\Delta>3/2; this is justified by seeing that the leading IR divergence contribution to the free energy from such an operator goes as β3−2​Δ\beta^{3-2\Delta} (at quadratic order in perturbation theory).

C.2 Perturbative action

We will now derive the subleading contribution to the perturbative free energy functional due to lattice-fermion mass couplings. Performing the same calculation as in the main text for lattice-monopole couplings, we enter the weak coupling regime g2​β3−2​ΔΦ​|h→|≪1g^{2}\beta^{3-2\Delta_{\Phi}}|\vec{h}|\ll 1 and perform a perturbative expansion of the free energy ⟨Sm2⟩/β​V\langle S_{m}^{2}\rangle/\beta V. Using the explicitly derived structure of the coupling, we find

⟨Sm2⟩QED3β​V\displaystyle\frac{\langle S^{2}_{m}\rangle_{\mathrm{QED}_{3}}}{\beta V} =−m2∫d3xϵa​b​c​ϵa​d​e​hb​hd∗​hc​he∗|x|2​ΔM\displaystyle=-m^{2}\int\differential[3]{x}\,\frac{\epsilon^{abc}\epsilon^{ade}\,h_{b}h_{d}^{*}\,h_{c}h_{e}^{*}}{|x|^{2\Delta_{M}}}
=cΔM​m2​β3−2​ΔM​(|h→⋅h→|2−|h→|4).\displaystyle=c_{\Delta_{M}}m^{2}\beta^{3-2\Delta_{M}}\left(|\vec{h}\cdot\vec{h}|^{2}-|\vec{h}|^{4}\right). (75)

This is IR-divergent if the exponent ΔM<3/2\Delta_{M}<3/2, which is compatible with large-NN calculations and within the range of values suggested by the conformal bootstrap [37]. Assuming this condition is satisfied, this subleading divergent contribition will be minimised by states satisfying h→⋅h→=0\vec{h}\cdot\vec{h}=0.

If this condition ΔM<3/2\Delta_{M}<3/2 is not satisfied, we would still expect the perturbative action to have only a SO⁡(3)\mathrm{SO(3)} symmetry which is inherited from the SO​(3)valley\mathrm{SO(3)}_{\mathrm{valley}} symmetry of the effective action. This inevitably occurs at higher order in perturbation theory, where the monopole-monopole and monopole-mass terms produce additional divergent contributions proportional to 𝒞⁡(β)​(|h→⋅h→|2−|h→|4)\mathcal{C}(\beta)(|\vec{h}\cdot\vec{h}|^{2}-|\vec{h}|^{4}) [79]. At quadratic order there is a contribution from the M×MM\times M OPE channel above, giving 𝒞(2)​(β)=c2​β3−2​ΔM\mathcal{C}^{(2)}(\beta)=c_{2}\,\beta^{3-2\Delta_{M}}. At higher order there are contributions from the following channels: Φ†×(M×Φ)→Φ†×Φ\Phi^{\dagger}\times(M\times\Phi)\to\Phi^{\dagger}\times\Phi is asymptotically 𝒞(3)​(β)=c3​β6−2​ΔΦ−ΔM\mathcal{C}^{(3)}(\beta)=c_{3}\,\beta^{6-2\Delta_{\Phi}-\Delta_{M}}; and the channel (Φ†×Φ)×(Φ†×Φ)→M×M(\Phi^{\dagger}\times\Phi)\times(\Phi^{\dagger}\times\Phi)\to M\times M contributes 𝒞(4)​(β)=c4​β9−4​ΔΦ\mathcal{C}^{(4)}(\beta)=c_{4}\,\beta^{9-4\Delta_{\Phi}}. We can constrain c2∼m2>0c_{2}\sim m^{2}>0 and c4∼g2​(CΦ​ΦM)2>0c_{4}\sim g^{2}(C_{\Phi\Phi}^{M})^{2}>0 to be positive, but the sign of c3c_{3} cannot be fixed in this way. There will be multiple additional contributions at this order (e.g. from ⟨Sg2⟩2/β​V\langle S_{g}^{2}\rangle^{2}/\beta V) which produce the potential |h→|4|\vec{h}|^{4}, leaving the sign of this coefficient in the effective action indeterminate. However we predict that the leading contributions to the |h→⋅h→|2|\vec{h}\cdot\vec{h}|^{2} term is positive.

Appendix D Numerical Simulations

We use the density matrix renormalization group algorithm (DMRG) [46, 86, 87] on infinite cylinders [48, 88, 89] to obtain the ground state of the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} Heisenberg model on a triangular lattice. The lattice is wrapped onto the cylindrical geometry by closing the boundary conditions periodically along the circumference Ly≡LL_{y}\equiv L. There are several possible ways that the periodic closing of the lattice can be achieved. In this work, we use the Y​C​Ly−0YC{L_{y}}-0 geometry [92, 91], where n=0n=0 determines the detailed boundary condition. The lattice sites 𝒓{{\bm{r}}} and 𝒓+Ly​𝒂2−n​𝒂1{{\bm{r}}}+L_{y}{{\bm{a}}}_{2}-n{{\bm{a}}}_{1} are thereby identified. We use U⁡(1)U(1)-charge conservation for all numerical simulations discussed in this work. We use the setup of infinite matrix product states (MPS) [86, 87] and optimize the ground state running infinite DMRG (iDMRG) on unit cells of size Ly×3L_{y}\times 3, where Lx=3L_{x}=3 denotes the number of rings in the cylinder geometry.

When optimizing the ground state of the two-dimensional Hamiltonian on the lattice, special care has to be taken when we consider a geometry with an even circumference LyL_{y}. The isotropic J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} Heisenberg model on even cylinders comprises two different topological sectors in the putative quantum spin liquid phase [128, 92]. The iDMRG algorithm in this case finds the even sector in which the entanglement spectrum on the bonds is symmetric around the total SzS_{z}-quantum number qz=0q_{z}=0. One can transition into the odd sector by adiabatically inserting a flux of 2​π2\pi through the cylinder [91]. In this process, the couplings of the model acquire complex phases along the circumference. The final state’s entanglement spectrum is symmetric around qz=12q_{z}=\frac{1}{2} which can be understood as a spinon quasiparticle with Sz=±12S_{z}=\pm\frac{1}{2} residing on each boundary [128]. To find the ground state for the Ly=6L_{y}=6-cylinder, we apply this protocol referred to as the flux-insertion method.

Alternatively, one can enforce a preference for odd dimer coverings on cylinders with even LyL_{y} by omitting a single site on each of the outermost cylinder rings of the unit cell for the first iDMRG sweeps before restoring the full model [92, 91] and having the algorithms optimize the ground state MPS until convergence. We refer to this protocol in contrast to the flux-insertion as the odd-sector method. We ensured that for sufficiently large bond dimensions, the energies obtained on Ly=6L_{y}=6 by the two distinct methods described above agree.

Starting from the ground state of the undistorted model, we can adiabatically turn on the distortion parameter δ\delta and modify the couplings of the Hamiltonian according to the pattern generated by a certain momentum 𝑸{{\bm{Q}}}. The parameter δ\delta controls the strength of the distortion. The full 12-site unit cell pattern in real-space is obtained from equation (40) as follows:

𝒓i=𝑹i+2​δ3​∑a=1,2,3sa​𝒌^a​sin⁡[𝒌a⋅𝒓i+2​π​(a−1)3],{{\bm{r}}}_{i}={{\bm{R}}}_{i}+\frac{2\delta}{\sqrt{3}}\sum_{a=1,2,3}s_{a}\hat{{\bm{k}}}_{a}\,\sin\left[{\bm{k}}_{a}\cdot{\bm{r}}_{i}+\frac{2\pi\,(a-1)}{3}\right], (76)

where 𝑹i{{\bm{R}}}_{i} denotes the undistorted position of site ii and δ\delta measures the magnitude of the distortion. All other patterns are generated via the formula

𝒓i=𝑹i+δ​(cos⁡[𝑸⋅𝑹i+θ]sin⁡[𝑸⋅𝑹i+θ]){{\bm{r}}}_{i}={{\bm{R}}}_{i}+\delta\begin{pmatrix}\cos[{{\bm{Q}}}\cdot{{\bm{R}}}_{i}+\theta]\\ \sin[{{\bm{Q}}}\cdot{{\bm{R}}}_{i}+\theta]\end{pmatrix} (77)

where the phase θ\theta is an additional parameter that gives rise to the various patterns for each momentum 𝑸{{\bm{Q}}} discussed in Section VI.2.1. The precise phases used for different distortion patterns are given in Figs. 9 and 10 alongside the real-space modification of the couplings (for a value δ=0.1\delta=0.1 for demonstration purposes).

For the investigation of the system size dependence, the simulated pattern at the commensurate monopole distortion for a single 𝑲2\frac{{{\bm{K}}}}{2}-momentum was taken as the negative −𝒌3=𝑲32-{{\bm{k}}}_{3}=\frac{{{\bm{K}}}_{3}}{2} with a phase of θ=16\theta=\frac{1}{6}. For the sake of readability, the corresponding data points in the figures have been named 𝒌3{{\bm{k}}}_{3}. The same naming convention has been chosen for the discussions in the main text. The pattern generated by 𝒌3{{\bm{k}}}_{3} in contrast to −𝒌3-{{\bm{k}}}_{3} would be mirrored along the 𝒂2{{\bm{a}}}_{2}-axis of the lattice, which is an irrelevant modification in terms of the physics of the system.

Fig. 4 shows the energy response for various patterns under adiabatic increase of the distortion δ\delta. The 𝑴{{\bm{M}}}-point patterns as shown in Fig. 9(c),  Figs. 10 (b–c) have different orientations on the cylinder with slightly differing energy responses. Fig. 4 therefore shows the averaged energy response over all three orientations. The shaded area indicates the range of the energy gain for the different orientations on the cylinder as shown explicitly in Fig. 8.

To check convergence in the virtual bond dimension χ\chi of the matrix product state, we can store the state along with the environments of the infinite DMRG simulation and restart the optimization under an increase of the bond dimension. The saving of the environments is necessary to ensure that the algorithm does not fall back into a possibly wrong topological sector.

In Fig. 8 and Figs. 11–12, we show the convergence for L=3L=3 and L=6L=6 for various patterns. The real-space distortions of the couplings alongside the spin-spin correlations ⟨S→i⋅S→j⟩\langle{\vec{S}}_{i}\cdot{\vec{S}}_{j}\rangle resulting from the numerically obtained ground states are shown in Fig. 9. As can be deduced from the figures, the energy difference is already extremely well-converged for intermediate bond dimensions of a few thousand. The absolute ground state energy, however, is not necessarily so well-converged for all circumferences and bond dimensions. Despite this, we have confidence in our results for the energy gain (even for small values 𝒪⁡(10−10)\mathcal{O}(10^{-10})) because of the stricter convergence criteria applied to the DMRG algorithm.

Note that the size of the unit cell in xx-direction, denoted by LxL_{x}, needs to be chosen in accordance with the pattern we simulate. More precisely, whereas the patterns for 𝑲{{\bm{K}}}-points can be fitted on any multiple of three, i.e. Ly×3L_{y}\times 3 is sufficient for the unit cell size to have a commensurate geometry (given that LyL_{y} itself is a multiple of three), the distortion patterns generated by the 𝑴{{\bm{M}}}-points or 𝑲2\frac{{\bm{K}}}{2} momenta, require an extent of Lx=6L_{x}=6 (or multiples thereof).

In contrast to Ly=3L_{y}=3 and Ly=6L_{y}=6, the circumference of Ly=9L_{y}=9 is more challenging as the computational complexity grows exponentially in LyL_{y}. In particular, the DMRG simulation tends to converge to semistable states that can change abruptly when bond dimension is insufficient. For small distortion strengths δ\delta, the convergence is more stable for the accessible bond dimensions. In Fig. 13, we show data for various patterns for Ly=9L_{y}=9, which appear to converge for two of the three patterns studied for a bond dimension of χ=6000\chi=6000 and in the case of the 𝑲{{\bm{K}}}-point for χ=7000\chi=7000.

Appendix E Phonon spectral function

In this section, we will evaluate the effect of fluctuations of the stable, quantum-critical DSL phase on the spectrum of the phonons. At zero-temperature we find a continuous spectrum of phonons [110] with a divergent spectral weight as ω→0\omega\to 0. As large temperature, the analysis in the main text shows there should instead be a well-defined pole in the phonon propagator with an energy that corresponds to a renormalized phonon frequency. We expect this pole to move towards zero as the spin-Peierls temperature is approached. We supplement the perturbative self-consistent analysis of the phonon self energy [given in Eq. (60)] with a full evaluation of the phonon spectral function. This provides a confirmation that the spectrum is described by a Kohn-anomaly-like dip at large temperatures, which will go to zero frequency at the spin-Peierls transition.

To describe this effect, we first effectively integrate-out the VBS-monopole fluctuations of the DSL to produce the dressed propagator of the phonons at quadratic order [110],

G⁡(ω,𝒌)=1ω0​(𝒌)2−g2​|𝒌a|2​ρ−1​χ​(ω,𝒌)−ω2G(\omega,{\bm{k}})=\frac{1}{\omega_{0}({\bm{k}})^{2}-g^{2}|{\bm{k}}_{a}|^{2}\rho^{-1}\chi(\omega,{\bm{k}})-\omega^{2}} (78)

where the bare phonon dispersion ω0​(𝒌)2=𝒦𝒌2/ρ\omega_{0}({\bm{k}})^{2}=\mathcal{K}_{{\bm{k}}}^{2}/\rho [Eq. (23)]. The phonon spectral function is given by S⁡(ω,𝒌)=2​Im⁡D⁡(ω+i​ϵ,𝒌)S(\omega,{\bm{k}})=2\operatorname{Im}D(\omega+\mathrm{i}\epsilon,{\bm{k}}). The spin-VBS channel susceptibility has the following form at zero temperature χ⁡(ω,𝒌)=[c2​|𝒌a−𝒌|2−ω2]−(3/2−ΔΦ)\chi(\omega,{\bm{k}})=[c^{2}|{\bm{k}}_{a}-{\bm{k}}|^{2}-\omega^{2}]^{-(3/2-\Delta_{\Phi})} featuring a divergent continuum of excitations at ω>c​|𝒌−𝒌a|\omega>c|{\bm{k}}-{\bm{k}}_{a}| (where cc is some emergent “speed of light”), but is not generally known at finite temperature. One can write generally χ⁡(ω,𝒌)=T2​ΔΦ−3​Φ​(ω/T,c​|𝒌−𝒌a|/T),\chi(\omega,{\bm{k}})=T^{2\Delta_{\Phi}-3}\,\Phi({\omega}/{T},{c|{\bm{k}}-{\bm{k}}_{a}|}/{T}), where Φ\Phi is an unknown universal scaling function and constrain it in the large-temperature limit [129, 130, 131]. While even asymptotic results for the frequency-dependent susceptibility at finite-TT are not exactly known, for illustrative purposes we heuristically assume a form similar to the expansion obtained by Sachdev and Ye [129]. In Figure. 14, we plot the phonon spectral function, in the exact, zero-temperature limit (left) as well as a high-TT asymptotic result (right). We expect a temperature-dependent softening of the phonon mode towards zero at the spin-Peierls temperature. This is accompanied by the emergence of a sharp divergent continuum of excitations which blurs with the mode at low energies. A better understanding of the scaling form Φ\Phi would allow a prediction of how this mode approaches zero, a feature which can be experimentally and numerically probed.
